MUJAHID:v1p112/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p112/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p112/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses the question about reviving the ruined town as asking how God will revive it, and says the passerby was a prophet named Armiya.

MUQATIL:2:259#2/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r1.claim: Nanshizuhā means revive the donkey's bones; Muqatil links the same root in 21:21 with raising the dead.

MUQATIL:2:259#2/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r2.claim: Once Ezra saw how God revives the dead, he prostrated and affirmed God's power over everything, including resurrection.

MUQATIL:2:259#2/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259#2/r3.claim: Ezra returned to find his family dead and his house sold and rebuilt; his descendants recognized him, and God granted him knowledge after raising him.

MUQATIL:2:259/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259/r1.claim: Nebuchadnezzar deported Babylon's people, including the Israelite scholar Ezra; Ezra passed the ruined village of Sabur by the Tigris between Wasit and Mada'in.

MUQATIL:2:259/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259/r2.claim: Ezra's question about reviving the village expressed a wish to witness resurrection, not doubt; this parallels Abraham's request to see how God revives the dead.

MUQATIL:2:259/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259/r3.claim: God caused Ezra and his donkey to die for one hundred years, then raised Ezra late in the day with his fruit and drink unchanged.

MUQATIL:2:259/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259/r4.claim: His preserved food and drink demonstrate that they had not changed over the century; Muqatil links this to the description of unaltered water and milk in Muhammad.

MUQATIL:2:259/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:259/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:259/r5.claim: The donkey's scattered bones reassembled in sequence, received sinews, nerves, hair, and spirit, and it rose braying before Ezra.

FARRA:v1p173/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r1.claim: The poem's سنهاء is an old palm and رجبية a palm near collapse, propped with stones; it supports pronouncing the final هاء when connected.

FARRA:v1p173/r10.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r10.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r10.claim: فصرهن may mean cut them or turn them toward you; cut is not well established in either pronunciation, so the author tentatively links it to صريت with a shifted ياء.

FARRA:v1p173/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r2.claim: The و in ولنجعلك anticipates an implied verb: We did this in order to make you a sign; this construction is frequent in the Quran.

FARRA:v1p173/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r3.claim: The man was revived with black hair and beard while his grandsons were gray, making him a sign for people.

FARRA:v1p173/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r4.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
FARRA:v1p173/r4.claim: Zayd ibn Thabit read ننشزها, meaning to move the bones into their places.

FARRA:v1p173/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v1p173/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas read ننشرها as giving life, citing ثم إذا شاء أنشره; al-Hasan also read ننشرها, taking it as spreading and folding.

FARRA:v1p173/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r6.claim: The author favors أنشر الله الموتى فنشروا for revival, citing al-A'sha and a Banū al-Harith usage where recovery is described as نشر.

FARRA:v1p173/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v1p173/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas read أعلم in the jussive and cited the reading قيل له اعلم in أبي and عبدالله's codices; he asked whether this man was better than Abraham, who was told واعلم.

FARRA:v1p173/r8.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r8.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r8.claim: The common reading أعلم is good: it means that, once the matter became clear, the man said I testify that God has power over everything; the alternative is also clear.

FARRA:v1p173/r9.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p173/r9.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p173/r9.claim: The common reading has صاد with ḍamma; Abdullah's followers use kasra, a dialect found among Hudhayl and Sulaym.

MAJAZ:v1p79/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p79/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p79/r4.claim: Khāwiyah means without inhabitants, and ʿalā ʿurūshihā means upon its houses and buildings.

MAJAZ:v1p79/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p79/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p79/r5.claim: Lam yatasannah means years have not passed over the food to change it; on the sana derivation it is not from asina, which would yield yata'asan.

MAJAZ:v1p79/r6.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p79/r6.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p79/r6.claim: One reading, nanshuruhā, means revive them; those reading nunshizuhā understand raising the bones together.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r1.claim: Wahb says Moses's Ark was about three cubits by two and contained Moses's staff and the Sakina, a spirit from God that spoke to clarify disputes.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r2.speaker: علي
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r2.claim: Ali describes the Sakina as having a humanlike face and then as a gently fluttering breeze.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p100/r3.claim: Mujahid says the Sakina had two wings and a tail like a cat's.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r1.claim: Qatada identifies the figure as Ezra: he passed a ruined village, wondered how God would revive it, died at the start of the day, and returned at its end after a century.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r2.claim: He explains لم يتسنه as meaning that the food and drink did not change.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r3.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p106/r3.claim: Ibn Sirin reports that Zayd ibn Thabit recited the phrase with ننشزها, meaning raise or join the bones.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107#4/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107#4/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107#4/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the statement acknowledging God's power was said to the man after the resurrection became clear to him.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107/r1.speaker: قتادة والحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p107/r1.claim: They report that Ezra's eyes were the first part of him created, so he could watch his bones and flesh come together.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r1.claim: Wahb identifies the passerby as Jeremiah, who saw Jerusalem ruined after its destruction and asked how God would revive it; God made him die for a century.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r2.claim: Israelites began rebuilding seventy years after his death and completed the city by the hundredth year; Jeremiah returned to find it restored.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r3.claim: Jeremiah watched the bones join, then acquire sinews and flesh, and acknowledged God's power.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r4.claim: His figs in a basket and water in a vessel had not changed during the century.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r5.claim: After the Ark was returned, God sent illness among the Israelites; a prophet, perhaps Daniel, was told its removal would lift the disease.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r6.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r6.claim: The sign was that two unworked, difficult cows would willingly take the yoke and pull the Ark cart wherever God directed.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r7.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r7.claim: Four angels drove the cows; they sped toward Jerusalem, then stopped at its edge, broke their traces, and left the Ark.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r8.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r8.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r8.claim: David rejoiced and danced at the recovered Ark; Wahb explains the movement as dance, and David divorced the wife who reproached him for it.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r9.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r9.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p99/r9.claim: After Nebuchadnezzar burned the Torah, God sent an angel with a chamber of light, which restored it for Ezra letter by letter.

AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r2.claim: In أو كالذي مر على قرية, the comparative كاف is extra, linking the example back to the challenge about Abraham; likewise ليس كمثله شيء means ليس كهو, since God has no likeness.

AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r3.claim: The hāʾ in لم يتسنه may be a pause marker and then drop in connected speech, like اخشه; some retain it in connection as original, which is the reading Akhfash follows.

AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r4.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r4.claim: The word سنة may derive from waw or hāʾ; Arabic forms such as سنية, سنيهة, أسنتوا, مساناة, and مسانهة preserve the competing derivations.

AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r5.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r5.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p196#2/r5.claim: Akhfash relates ننشزها to نشر, opposite of folding; others use ننشرها to mean raise, supported by نشز هذا and أنشزته.

AKHFASH:v1p198/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p198/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p198/r1.claim: The indicative أعلم means I know when the speaker refers to himself; the jussive اعلم is an imperative to another, or self-admonition, and is semantically better but less often read. Akhfash follows the common nominative reading.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r1.claim: The opening compares the passerby with someone who disputed Abraham about his Lord, in a rhetorical question expressing wonder.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r2.claim: Khawiya means ruined; ʿurūsh are roofs, which collapse first, followed by the walls falling onto them.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p94/r3.claim: Then God raised the man means that He brought him back to life.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r1.claim: The man is made a sign and proof of God's power; the text implies “We did this.”

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r2.claim: With rāʾ, nanshuruhā means revive the bones; Arabic says God revived the dead.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r3.claim: With zāy, nanshuzuhā means move the bones toward one another and set them upright; the root also describes a wife rebelling against her husband.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads ننشرها with rāʾ, deriving it from spreading something after folding it, or using a form meaning revive.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r5.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r5.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p95/r5.claim: Although he has not heard this pairing of faʿala and afʿala forms, both anshara and nashara may mean revive.

TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r1.claim: The “or like the one” clause links by meaning to the preceding rhetorical question about the disputant with Abraham in 2:258, despite differing wording.

TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r2.claim: A Basran grammarian treated the kaf as extra, but al-Tabari rejects the claim because no Qur’anic element is meaningless.

TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r3.speaker: ناجية بن كعب، سليمان بن بريدة، قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p577#2/r3.claim: These reports identify the person who passed the ruined town as Ezra (ʿUzayr); Qatada says this was reported to them.

TAB-FULL:v4p580/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r1.speaker: الربيع، عكرمة، السدي، الضحاك، ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r1.claim: These authorities identify the passerby as Ezra (ʿUzayr).

TAB-FULL:v4p580/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r2.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq transmits the view that the man was Jeremiah and says Jeremiah was the Khidr, whose name among the Children of Israel was Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.

TAB-FULL:v4p580/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r3.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah saw Jerusalem destroyed and its books burned, then asked how God could revive it after its death.

TAB-FULL:v4p580/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v4p580/r4.claim: Ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr says the passerby was a prophet named Jeremiah.

TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه، قتادة، الضحاك، عكرمة، الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r1.claim: Several reports identify the ruined town as Jerusalem, with one saying Ezra came after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it; al-Dahhak calls it the Holy Land.

TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the town as the place where people fled a plague, died, and were revived; the passerby saw their bones and asked how God would bring them back.

TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p582#2/r3.claim: As with the passerby’s identity, the town cannot be identified with certainty from reliable evidence; the verse does not require a specific name.

TAB-FULL:v4p582/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r1.claim: Al-Tabari cannot establish the passerby’s name reliably: he may have been Ezra or Jeremiah, and identifying him is not the verse’s purpose.

TAB-FULL:v4p582/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r2.claim: The point is to expose those who deny resurrection: the man questioned how God could revive a town despite knowing that God first created it from nothing.

TAB-FULL:v4p582/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r3.claim: The account also establishes Muhammad’s prophethood to Quraysh and the Jews of Medina, since an unlettered messenger conveyed reports known only to the People of the Book.

TAB-FULL:v4p582/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p582/r4.claim: If naming the passerby were the purpose, the text would state it decisively; instead, it aims to condemn the question he uttered.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r1.claim: He notes that related forms are used for a woman after childbirth, a house, and a hollow body, though he considers the stated usage more eloquent.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r2.claim: ʿUrush means buildings or houses; ʿarsh is singular, and the related verb means to build, as in 7:137 and the name for Mecca’s tents and buildings.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses khawiya as ruined.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses the town as ruined.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r5.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r5.claim: Al-Rabiʿ says Ezra passed the town after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it.

TAB-FULL:v4p584/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r6.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p584/r6.claim: Al-Suddi says the town had collapsed onto its roofs.

TAB-FULL:v4p586/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r1.claim: Some interpreters understand the question as doubt about God’s ability; God answers by showing resurrection in the questioner himself and restoration of the town he had seen destroyed.

TAB-FULL:v4p586/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r2.claim: The man had known the town when full of inhabitants, then saw it empty after killing and captivity had scattered them and its homes were ruined.

TAB-FULL:v4p586/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p586/r3.claim: God demonstrated His power through the man’s body and food and drink, then by making him witness what had seemed impossible, prompting his confession that God can do everything.

TAB-FULL:v4p588/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r1.claim: Wahb recounts that God chose and purified Jeremiah before birth, sent him to warn Israel’s king and people, and announced their coming destruction because they persisted in sins and forgot deliverance from Sennacherib.

TAB-FULL:v4p588/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r2.claim: Jeremiah grieved at the announced destruction and vowed never to ask God to destroy Israel; God promised Jerusalem and Israel would not be destroyed until Jeremiah himself ordered it.

TAB-FULL:v4p588/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p588/r3.claim: Israel nevertheless persisted in wrongdoing for three more years; worldly concerns then distracted them, and reminders of the afterlife ceased.

TAB-FULL:v4p590/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p590/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p590/r1.claim: In Wahb’s account, Nebuchadnezzar approached Jerusalem; an angel posing as an Israelite twice asked Jeremiah how to deal with relatives who spurned his kindness, and Jeremiah urged continued kindness and prayer.

TAB-FULL:v4p590/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p590/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p590/r2.claim: When Jerusalem was surrounded, the king asked Jeremiah about God’s promise; Jeremiah remained confident, but the disguised angel returned saying Israel’s latest deeds angered him and asking Jeremiah to pray against them.

TAB-FULL:v4p591/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p591/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p591/r1.claim: Jeremiah prayed that Israel be preserved if righteous or destroyed if sinful; a heavenly strike hit the Temple, and God told Jeremiah it followed his repeated verdicts. Nebuchadnezzar then destroyed Jerusalem, killed and deported Israelites, and took captives to Babylon.

TAB-FULL:v4p591/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p591/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه اليماني
TAB-FULL:v4p591/r2.claim: After Babylon’s destruction, Jeremiah returned with a donkey, grape drink, and figs; God killed and concealed him and the donkey for a century, then revived him, preserved his food, rebuilt the donkey, and showed him the resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v4p594/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r1.claim: Wahb gives another account: God sent Jeremiah from Egypt to Jerusalem; he saw its ruins, questioned how God would revive it, then slept as God withheld his soul for one hundred years.

TAB-FULL:v4p594/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r2.claim: After seventy years, a Persian king was ordered to rebuild Jerusalem with three hundred overseers and three hundred thousand workers; thirty years later Jeremiah’s spirit returned as the city was restored.

TAB-FULL:v4p594/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p594/r3.claim: At the century’s end, Jeremiah saw his food and drink unchanged and watched his donkey’s bones and his own body restored, learning that God can do everything.

TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r1.claim: Here kam asks for a numerical duration and is accusative governed by labithta; the question asks how long the man remained dead.

TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r2.claim: The man could have been Jeremiah, Ezra, or another person described by the report; his initial estimate of a day reflected being taken at dawn and revived near sunset a century later.

TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r3.claim: He first thought the sun had set and said a day, then noticed some sunlight remained and corrected himself to “or part of a day”; aw can mean rather, as in 37:147.

TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r4.claim: Qatada says the man died in the forenoon, revived before sunset after a hundred years, and corrected his estimate when he saw some sun remained.

TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r5.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p596#2/r5.claim: Al-Rabiʿ briefly repeats that God killed the man for one hundred years and then revived him.

TAB-FULL:v4p596/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r1.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah saw Jerusalem and its books destroyed, asked how God could revive it, and was restored after a century; the Israelites rebuilt the city during the final thirty years.

TAB-FULL:v4p596/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r2.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah watched the bones join and acquire sinews and flesh; his food was figs and his drink water, both unchanged.

TAB-FULL:v4p596/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p596/r3.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the passerby as Ezra, who questioned how the town could be revived without denying or doubting God’s power; God killed him and his donkey for a century and preserved his figs, grapes, and juice.

TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r1.claim: The food and drink were unchanged by the passing years; reports variously describe them as figs and grapes with water, grapes and figs with wine, or figs with wine.

TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r2.claim: One reading omits the h in connected recitation but retains it at a pause, treating it as an added connective letter and deriving the word from tasannaytu; this was the general Kufan reading.

TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r3.claim: Another reading retains h in both connection and pause as an original root letter, making the verb jussive after lam; it was the general Medinan and Hijazi reading.

TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p598#2/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers retaining h in both positions because it appears in the codices and has a sound linguistic explanation: the food had not aged or changed.

TAB-FULL:v4p598/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p598/r1.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v4p598/r1.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports that the passerby reached Jerusalem destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, asked how it could be restored, and died; he was reportedly raised before sunset after one hundred years.

TAB-FULL:v4p600/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r1.claim: A cited poem supports h as an original part of the word for year; a Qur’anic letter with a valid linguistic basis cannot be deleted in recitation.

TAB-FULL:v4p600/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r2.claim: The h in this word cannot be dismissed as a pause-only addition like the unambiguously extra h in “iqtadih” or “kitabiyah,” because it may be original.

TAB-FULL:v4p600/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r3.claim: Even letters added for pause can be pronounced in connected speech, but this case remains distinct because the h in yatasannah may be part of the root.

TAB-FULL:v4p600/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r4.speaker: عثمان
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r4.claim: When Zayd asked whether the text should read with h, Uthman ordered that the h be written.

TAB-FULL:v4p600/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r5.speaker: أبي بن كعب
TAB-FULL:v4p600/r5.claim: A report about Uthman’s codex review says he added the h to yatasannah after correcting other written forms; Zayd was reported to agree.

TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r1.claim: Mujahid reads yatasannah as “did not become foul-smelling”; he identifies the food as figs and the drink as wine in a jar.

TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r2.claim: Al-Tabari says Mujahid and those sharing his view derive the word from masnun, “changed in odor,” but he has already shown this derivation is wrong.

TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p605#2/r3.claim: Deriving the form from asin, “stale,” in 47:15 also fails: the expected form would be yata’asan, or yatasan without a doubled n if the hamza were dropped.

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r1.claim: Wahb says yatasannah means “did not change.”

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r2.claim: Qatada glosses yatasannah as “did not change.”

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says the figs, grapes, and juice remained sweet and unchanged for a hundred years, without souring or fermenting.

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak says the food and drink did not change despite a hundred years passing.

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses yatasannah as “did not change.”

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r6.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r6.claim: ʿIkrima glosses yatasannah as “did not change.”

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd says the food and drink did not change over one hundred years.

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r8.speaker: بكر بن مضر
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r8.claim: Bكر ibn Mudar transmits a story that Jeremiah returned from Egypt to ruined Jerusalem, where his tethered donkey and baskets of figs and grapes remained unchanged.

TAB-FULL:v4p605/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r9.speaker: سلم الخواص
TAB-FULL:v4p605/r9.claim: Salm al-Khawwas says the food and drink were baskets of grapes and figs and a wineskin of juice.

TAB-FULL:v4p607/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r1.claim: One interpretation takes “look at your donkey” as a command to witness God resurrecting the donkey and restoring its bones.

TAB-FULL:v4p607/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r2.claim: Wahb recounts that the donkey’s bones joined, flesh covered them, and it stood alive; the drink and figs remained unchanged throughout the century.

TAB-FULL:v4p607/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r3.claim: Al-Suddi describes scattered donkey bones being reassembled, clothed with flesh and blood, then given life when an angel breathed into its nostril.

TAB-FULL:v4p607/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r4.claim: On this reading, the verse omits “the bones of it” after “your donkey,” since the intended referent is clear; “the bones” then substitutes for the implied pronoun.

TAB-FULL:v4p607/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p607/r5.claim: Another reported view says God addressed him after giving him life in one organ, before resurrecting the donkey.

TAB-FULL:v4p609/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r1.claim: Mujahid says the man was an Israelite whose spirit first entered his eyes, allowing him to watch both his whole creation and the donkey’s resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v4p609/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r2.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r2.claim: Ibn Jurayj describes the eyes receiving spirit first, then the body’s bones, sinews, veins, flesh, skin, and hair being reassembled as the man watched.

TAB-FULL:v4p609/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r3.claim: In Ibn Jurayj’s account, the donkey’s bones reunite and its aged body revives; the man’s food was a bunch of grapes and his drink wine.

TAB-FULL:v4p609/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r4.claim: Wahb says life returned to Jeremiah’s eye while the rest of his body remained dead; he saw his food, drink, and donkey unchanged.

TAB-FULL:v4p609/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r5.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p609/r5.claim: Al-Dahhak says the donkey and provisions remained as they were, and the man’s head was the first part revived so he could watch the rest take shape.

TAB-FULL:v4p611/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r1.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r1.claim: Qatada reports that God first created the man’s head and eyes, then joined the bones while the Prophet’s eyes witnessed it.

TAB-FULL:v4p611/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r2.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r2.claim: Al-Rabi reports that the donkey remained intact; the man’s eyes formed first, and he watched the bones reconnect.

TAB-FULL:v4p611/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p611/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says the spirit was placed in the man’s sight and tongue so he could summon each bone to its counterpart; the body was rebuilt and animated before the ruined village.

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r1.claim: “To make you a sign for the people” means God caused him to die for a hundred years and then raised him.

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r2.claim: The waw before the purpose-lām makes the purpose a condition of the preceding act; without it, the sense would be “look at your donkey in order to make you a sign.”

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r3.claim: His revival is evidence against those who doubt divine power: God alone controls death, life, destruction, creation, provision, and deprivation.

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r4.speaker: الأعمش
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r4.claim: Al-Aʿmash explains the sign as the man returning young while his children had become old.

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r5.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r5.claim: Al-Suddi says he returned to find his house sold and those who knew him dead; his family recognized him as ʿUzayr and returned the house.

TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613#2/r6.claim: The verse’s general point is that God made him a proof to his children, community, and others who knew he had died and then saw him restored.

TAB-FULL:v4p613/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r1.speaker: بكر بن مضر
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r1.claim: A report attributed to books says God killed Jeremiah for a century, then raised him while his donkey stood alive; his sight and spirit had returned thirty years earlier, and he saw Jerusalem restored.

TAB-FULL:v4p613/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r2.claim: On that view, the command concerns the man’s own bones, rebuilt after decay and clothed with flesh, making his revival a lesson in how God revives towns and their people.

TAB-FULL:v4p613/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r3.claim: Al-Tabari prefers that God raised the questioner and showed him, in himself, his food, and his donkey, a visible counterpart to the town’s revival.

TAB-FULL:v4p613/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p613/r4.claim: The command to inspect “the bones” includes all bones within sight, since both the man’s and donkey’s bones had decayed; neither referent alone accounts for the wording.

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r1.claim: The Kufan reading ننشزها with zāy means raising the bones from the earth and returning them to their bodily places; the root denotes rising or elevation.

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses the zāy reading as “bringing them out.”

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r3.claim: Al-Suddi glosses the zāy reading as “moving them.”

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r4.claim: The Medinan reading ننشرها with rāʾ means reviving the bones; Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd explain it as God bringing them to life.

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r5.claim: Some readers support the rāʾ reading by linking it to the Qur’anic phrase “when He wills, He raises him.”

TAB-FULL:v4p615/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p615/r6.claim: A reading with initial fatḥa and rāʾ is not commendable: Arabic uses God as the agent who revives the dead, not “the dead revived” with this form.

TAB-FULL:v4p619/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r1.speaker: الأعشى
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r1.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s verse uses الناشر for a dead person who has revived, supporting the verb’s sense of becoming alive again.

TAB-FULL:v4p619/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r2.claim: Al-Tabari considers الإنشار and الإنشاز close in meaning: both describe restoring separated bones to their bodily places, so either transmitted reading is valid.

TAB-FULL:v4p619/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r3.claim: Even when الإنشار means reviving, here it means returning bones to their places, not restoring the departed spirit; the spirit enters after flesh is added.

TAB-FULL:v4p619/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r4.claim: The reading with fatḥa on the nūn and rāʾ is not acceptable because it is anomalous among Muslim readings and departs from correct, eloquent Arabic.

TAB-FULL:v4p619/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p619/r5.claim: An Arabic expression for a recurring skin disease, “it نشر,” was also heard to mean the condition returned or revived.

TAB-FULL:v4p620/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p620/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p620/r1.claim: In “then We clothe them,” the pronoun refers to the bones; clothing them means covering them with flesh as a garment covers a human body.

TAB-FULL:v4p620/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p620/r2.speaker: النابغة الجعدي
TAB-FULL:v4p620/r2.claim: Al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī calls Islam a cloak because it covered and removed what came before it.

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r1.claim: When the revival became visibly clear, the man recognized the divine power and said he now knew God could do everything.

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r2.claim: The Kufan reading وصل الألف with a jussive mīm is an imperative, “know”; ʿAbd Allāh’s reading explicitly has “it was said: know.”

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r3.speaker: هارون
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r3.claim: Harun reports that ʿAbd Allāh’s reading has “it was said: know,” as a divine command.

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas’s transmitted reading is “he said: know,” and he explains that the command was addressed to the revived man.

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r5.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r5.claim: Al-Rabi reports that after watching the bones join, the man was told to know that God can do everything.

TAB-FULL:v4p621/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p621/r6.claim: Other readers use a hamza and nominative mīm, reading the phrase as his own statement: “I now know that God can do everything.”

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r1.claim: Wahb says that after seeing God’s power, the man concluded that God can do everything.

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r2.claim: Qatada identifies the speaker as a prophet and says his conclusion followed the reassembly of the bones.

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says ʿUzayr made this statement when he saw God revive his donkey.

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak says the man watched each part join its counterpart before making the statement.

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r5.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the imperative reading because the surrounding commands tell the revived man what to inspect; after seeing the revival and preserved provisions, God commands him to recognize divine power.

TAB-FULL:v4p622/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p622/r6.claim: The imperative parallels God’s command to Abraham, after showing him how the dead are revived, to know that God is mighty and wise.

ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r1.claim: The verse is coordinated with the preceding discourse in meaning: ‘Have you considered someone who passed by a town?’ Qarya derives from gathering people, as water is gathered in a basin.

ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r2.claim: Abu ʿUbayda explains the town’s ʿurūsh as tents, the dwellings of Bedouins.

ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r3.speaker: غير أبي عبيدة
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r3.claim: Another authority explains the phrase as walls left standing without roofs.

ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r4.claim: Khāwiya means empty of inhabitants; the author favors the form khawat al-dār over khawayat.

ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p342/r5.claim: The root also describes a woman’s womb after birth or a man’s empty stomach; here the short-vowel form is used, with another verbal form also possible but less preferred.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and ʿĀṣim pronounce the thāʾ distinctly in every occurrence of كم لبثت/لبثتم; the other four readers assimilate it.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r2.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r2.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r2.claim: These readers retain the hāʾ in liaison in لم يتسنه and the listed parallel forms; all readers retain it at pause, and all keep it in the two further al-Ḥāqqa forms in both positions.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r3.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r3.speaker: حمزة
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r3.claim: Ḥamza drops the hāʾ in liaison in all the listed forms; like everyone, he retains it at pause.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r4.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r4.speaker: الكسائي
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r4.claim: Al-Kisāʾī drops the hāʾ in liaison only in لم يتسنه and اقتده, retaining it in the remaining listed forms.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r5.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r5.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r5.claim: These readers pronounce ننشرها with rāʾ and ḍamma on the first nūn; ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read ننشزها with zāy.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r6.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r6.speaker: أبان عن عاصم
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r6.claim: Abān transmits ننشرها from ʿĀṣim with fatḥa on the first nūn and ḍamma on shīn.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r7.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r7.speaker: عبد الوهاب عن أبان عن عاصم
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r7.claim: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's transmission through Abān from ʿĀṣim gives the same form as al-Ḥasan.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r8.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r8.speaker: عبيد الله بن علي عن نصر عن أبيه عن أبان عن عاصم
IBNMUJAHID:v1p188/r8.claim: A further transmission through ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿAlī reports the same form from Abān and ʿĀṣim.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p189/r1.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p189/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p189/r1.claim: These readers cut the alif in أعلم and use ḍamma on mīm; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī join the alif and use sukūn.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r1.claim: Ali identifies the passerby as the prophet Ezra, who left his city while young and came upon a ruined town; al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Burayda, and Qatada also identify him as Ezra.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r2.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r2.claim: A Syrian man gives a different identification: the person whom God caused to die for a hundred years was Hizqil ibn Buzā.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r3.claim: Ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr says the man was a prophet named Irmiya; Mujahid instead identifies him as an Israelite, and Wahb is reported to agree with Mujahid.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r4.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r4.claim: Qatada says the man was Ezra visiting Jerusalem after Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian destroyed it; al-Dahhak is reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r6.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r6.claim: Qatada explains that the ruined town had no one in it.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r7.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r7.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets its collapsed roofs as the roofs themselves; al-Suddi agrees.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r8.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p500/r8.claim: Qatada paraphrases the passerby's question as asking how God will rebuild the town after its ruin; al-Rabi ibn Anas gives the same interpretation.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r1.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r1.claim: Al-Suddi pictures Ezra arriving from Syria with a donkey, grapes, juice, and figs; on seeing the ruined town he gestured and asked how God would revive it, without denying or doubting resurrection.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r2.speaker: اسباط
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r2.claim: The report says God caused the man and his donkey to die, and a hundred years passed over them.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says God punished an Israelite for asking the question: the donkey stood beside him without food or drink for a hundred years while his food and drink remained nearby.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r4.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r4.claim: Qatada says the man died at the beginning of the day and was raised after a hundred years.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r5.claim: Wahb identifies the man as Jeremiah, who asked the question after Jerusalem and its books were destroyed; God restored his spirit after a century, when the city had been rebuilt, following an initial return of Israelites after seventy years and thirty years of rebuilding.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r6.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p501/r6.claim: Ali says that when Ezra was raised after a hundred years, his eyes were the first part of him created.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r1.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r1.claim: Al-Suddi says God then brought Ezra back to life.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r2.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r2.claim: Qatada says Ezra was raised at the end of the day; al-Rabi says he was raised before sunset.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r3.claim: Qatada says the man thought he had stayed a day, then saw the remaining sun and revised this to part of a day; al-Hasan and al-Rabi give a similar account.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r4.claim: Ali's account says Ezra's bones came together, were clothed with flesh, and received a spirit; returning to his city as a young man, he found his young shoemaker neighbor now old.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r5.claim: Qatada says Ezra's food was a basket of figs; Wahb ibn Munabbih and Mujahid are reported to give the same account.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r6.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r6.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the food as figs and grapes.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r7.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r7.claim: Wahb identifies the drink as water kept in a small vessel.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r8.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p502/r8.claim: Qatada identifies the drink as a skin filled with grape juice.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r1.claim: Mujahid identifies the food as a basket of figs and the drink as a skin of wine or juice.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says “it did not change” means the food and drink remained unchanged; al-Hasan, Mujahid, Wahb, Qatada, and others agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r3.claim: Al-Dahhak's report from Ibn Abbas stresses that food and drink remained unspoiled for a full hundred years, an extraordinary sign because they normally spoil sooner.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says the figs did not turn sour and the juice did not ferment over the hundred years; both remained lawful and unchanged.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r5.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r5.claim: Mujahid's second gloss of “لم يتسنه” is “it did not putrefy.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r6.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r6.claim: Abu Amr ibn al-Ala reads the word as “لم يتسن” and explains that the years had not passed over it.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r7.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r7.claim: Ikrima says the donkey's separated joints came together one by one and were then clothed with flesh.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r8.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r8.claim: Al-Suddi says the donkey had died and its bones had decayed.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r9.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r9.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p503/r9.claim: Mujahid says Ezra watched God bring the donkey back to life.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r1.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r1.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas says the donkey remained beside Ezra just as it was.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r2.claim: Ikrima says the man was raised young after 140 years, while his sons had become centenarian elders; al-A'mash and al-Minhal ibn Amr are reported to give the same contrast.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says God made the man a sign by showing him this lesson in his own person.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says Ezra returned to find his home rebuilt and his acquaintances dead; after proving his identity, his relatives vacated the house and returned it to him.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r5.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r5.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas glosses “a sign” as “a lesson.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p504/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “how We raise them” as making the bones stand up or rise, limb by limb.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r1.claim: Wahb says Ezra watched as the bones joined one another.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r2.claim: Al-Suddi explains the bones being raised as being moved and then clothed; a wind gathered the donkey's bones from hills and plains, where animals had scattered them, and assembled a fleshless skeleton before Ezra.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r3.speaker: أبو حفص مبشر بن عبيد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r3.claim: Abu Hafs Mubashshir ibn Ubayd reports a reading, “كيف ننشزها,” with the meaning “we raise them upright.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says God clothed the bones with flesh and blood, then an angel blew into the donkey's nostril and it brayed.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r5.claim: Ikrima describes the joined joints being clothed in flesh, then nerves and skin, before breath was blown into the donkey's nostril and it brayed.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r6.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p506/r6.claim: Al-Hasan says the eyes were created first, and Ezra watched the rest of his body form and the bones receive flesh so he would learn that God revives the dead and can do all things.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the statement “when it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that God is powerful over everything’” was said to the man.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r2.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v2p507/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq explains that God can do whatever He wills with His servants, whether punishment or forgiveness.

NAHHAS:v1p330/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p330/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p330/r3.claim: The strongest sense of لم يتسنه is that years did not change the food and drink; the readings vary in hā' and assimilation.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r1.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r1.claim: The zāy reading suits bones that remain intact: they are raised before being clothed in flesh, supported by the sense of resurrection after decay.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r2.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100#2/r2.claim: The rāʾ reading treats restoration as equally easy whether or not the bones have decayed, since God says Be and it is.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r1.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r1.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r1.claim: The thāʾ in كم لبثت may assimilate into tāʾ because the letters are close in articulation, or remain distinct according to the unaltered form.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r2.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r2.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r2.claim: Cut alif and indicative رفع makes أعلم the speaker's report about himself; joined alif and pause makes it God's command to the addressee.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r3.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r3.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r3.claim: Retaining the pause hāʾ in liaison follows the written consonant text; dropping it treats the hāʾ as a pause marker whose role is supplied by connection.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r4.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r4.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r4.claim: Some readers deliberately pause on the hāʾ to match both script and pronunciation; others vary between retaining and dropping it to show both are allowed.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r5.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r5.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r5.claim: The hāʾ may be original and jazm-sukūn, or derive from لم يتسنن after one nūn changes to alif and drops, with hāʾ added for pause; both explain that years did not alter it.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r6.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r6.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p100/r6.claim: Deriving لم يتسنه from أسن is mistaken, since that derivation would produce يتأسن.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, and Asim pronounce the ث clearly in كم لبثت and لبثتم throughout the Quran.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r2.claim: Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisai assimilate ث into ت throughout the Quran.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r3.claim: Clear pronunciation follows from the sounds' differing articulation zones; assimilation treats them as near-identical because they share tongue-tip contact and voicelessness, and ت is a subject suffix bound like part of the word.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p367#2/r4.claim: The assimilation is supported by ست, where Arabic assimilates dāl to ت despite their voicing difference, and by the assimilation of the middle of وتد in a variant.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r1.claim: These readers retain ه in liaison in all five listed words, including لم يتسنه; everyone retains it at pause.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r2.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r2.claim: Hamza deletes the h in liaison from all five words; al-Kisai deletes it in لم يتسنه and اقتده but retains it in the other three.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p368/r3.claim: سنة has two senses: a year or a drought, the opposite of fertility; the following discussion uses the drought sense to explain the verse's word.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r1.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r1.claim: The phrase عام السنة must mean a drought year, since reading it as a year of years would be tautological; poetry uses سنون for barren years.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r2.speaker: أوس
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p369/r2.claim: Aws describes the years around his land after the sacred month as drought-stricken and barren, glossing تلمع as lacking fertility and vegetation.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r1.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r1.claim: The word سنين has several plural patterns; the form in poetry is not a vocative truncation, but a plural like مأنة ومئون, with easing for rhyme.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r2.claim: لم يتسنه may derive from a noun ending in h, from سنة as in أسنتوا/سنوات, or from مسنون meaning changed, with an n assimilated or inverted.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r3.claim: Abu Amr al-Shaybani is reported to favor deriving لم يتسنه from سنة; on the proposed pause-h analyses its h should appear at pause and drop in connected speech.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p372/r4.claim: Retaining h in liaison is grammatically sound if h is the final radical of سنة, just as a final h remains in لم ينقه زيد and لم يجبه عمرو.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r1.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r1.claim: In اقتده, h can be a pronoun for the verbal noun: the command means اقتد الاقتداء, with the verbal noun supplied by the verb's meaning.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r2.claim: For ماليه, سلطانيه, and هيه, deleting h in liaison better fits Arabic; retaining it is also defensible when a complete phrase is treated like a rhyme at pause.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r3.speaker: حمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r3.claim: Hamza's deletion of all pause-h letters in liaison is strongest: if some people treat rhymes as ordinary speech, unmetered speech has even less reason to imitate rhymes.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r4.speaker: الكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p375/r4.claim: Al-Kisai takes a middle course, deleting h from يتسنه and اقتده but retaining it in the three phrase-final words; both choices are permissible.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r1.speaker: أحمد بن موسى
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r1.claim: Readers agree on h in كتابيه and حسابيه in liaison; this supports making phrase endings rhyme-like, not following the spelling of the codex.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r2.claim: Writing final tāʾ as h cannot explain pause-h readings: if script controlled pronunciation, feminine tāʾ and written alif elsewhere would also persist in liaison.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p377/r3.claim: Sibawayh records ثلاثة أربعة with a pause-like h in liaison; Abu Amr's clear n in ياسين والقرآن likewise reflects intending a pause between letter names.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p378/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p378/r1.speaker: سيبويه
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p378/r1.claim: Sibawayh does not treat such rare forms as productive analogies; extending them beyond number words and letter names would overgeneralize exceptional patterns.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r1.claim: They read ننشرها with first nūn damma and rāʾ; نشر in this reading means revive the bones, as in Quranic descriptions of resurrection.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r2.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r2.claim: These four read ننشزها with zāy; another report from Asim gives a rāʾ reading with an open first nūn and damma on shīn.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r3.claim: The rāʾ reading means revive: نشر, resurrection, and sending forth are close in sense, and wind too is described as spreading or bringing life.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r4.speaker: أبو زيد
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p379/r4.claim: Abu Zayd glosses أنشر الله الريح as sending it forth; the author relates this 'raising' to Quranic uses of baath and irsal for reviving.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r1.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r1.claim: The reported Asim reading ننشرها with open first nūn and damma on shīn can be causative, like drying the animal or lowering water, or can depict unfolding what death had folded.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p380/r2.claim: The zāy reading ننشزها means raise the bones, bringing them together for revival; نشوز is a wife's turning away from marital accord, a related sense of rising apart.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r1.claim: They read قال أعلم with a separate, hamzated alif and damma on mīm, as a statement: after witnessing revival, the speaker declares certain knowledge of God's power.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r2.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r2.claim: They join the hamza and read أعلم as an imperative, 'Know that God is capable of everything'; its force still amounts to a declaration of certainty.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p382#2/r3.claim: The imperative addresses the speaker's own soul as if it were another person, a recognized Arabic rhetorical practice illustrated with poetic self-address.

SULAMI:v1p77#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p77#3/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p77#3/r1.claim: Ibrahim asked to see resurrection in another person tactfully to witness wisdom and might; ʿUzayr wondered at divine power and was shown it in himself as correction, so each received an answer suited to his request.

SULAMI:v1p77#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p77#3/r2.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p77#3/r2.claim: Ibrahim phrased his request gently, while ʿUzayr was shown resurrection in himself to discipline him for wondering about God's power.

THALABI:v2p241/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r10.speaker: وهب وعكرمة وقتادة والربيع
THALABI:v2p241/r10.claim: They identify the ruined town as Jerusalem.

THALABI:v2p241/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r11.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v2p241/r11.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the town as the Holy Land.

THALABI:v2p241/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r12.speaker: ابن زيد
THALABI:v2p241/r12.claim: Ibn Zayd says the town was the place where thousands who feared death were destroyed after leaving their homes.

THALABI:v2p241/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r7.speaker: قتادة والربيع وعكرمة وناجية بن كعب وسليمان بن بريدة والضحاك والسدي وسليم الخواص
THALABI:v2p241/r7.claim: These authorities identify the traveler as Ezra (Uzayr ibn Sharya).

THALABI:v2p241/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r8.speaker: وهب بن منبه وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
THALABI:v2p241/r8.claim: They identify the traveler as Jeremiah ibn Khalfiya, from Aaron's line, and connect him with al-Khidr.

THALABI:v2p241/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p241/r9.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v2p241/r9.claim: Mujahid says the traveler was an unbeliever who doubted resurrection.

THALABI:v2p242/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r1.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v2p242/r1.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the town as the monastery of Sa'idabad.

THALABI:v2p242/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r2.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v2p242/r2.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the town as Salmabad.

THALABI:v2p242/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p242/r3.claim: Other suggested sites are the monastery of Harafil and the Grape Village, two farsakhs from Jerusalem.

THALABI:v2p242/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p242/r4.claim: Khawiya can describe a collapsed house or an emptied house; ʿurush are roofs and buildings, and the verse means roofs fell first and walls on top of them.

THALABI:v2p242/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p242/r5.claim: Another reading takes على to mean with; a poem is cited for that usage, and analogous wording occurs in al-Kahf and al-Hajj.

THALABI:v2p242/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p242/r6.speaker: وهب بن منبه عن محمد بن إسحاق
THALABI:v2p242/r6.claim: A long report identifies the traveler as Jeremiah: God chose and commissioned him to warn sinful Israel, inspired his sermon, and foretold a Babylonian destruction; Jeremiah pleaded not to witness it, and God made his consent the condition of their destruction.

THALABI:v2p243/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p243/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه عن محمد بن إسحاق
THALABI:v2p243/r1.claim: The report continues: Jeremiah refused consent to Israel's destruction, told a pious king, and the king accepted the possibility of punishment for their sins or pardon through mercy; the people then persisted in wrongdoing.

THALABI:v2p243/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p243/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p243/r2.claim: An angel twice posed as a wronged relative to Jeremiah, who urged him to treat his family well; during Babylon's siege, he later exposed their behavior as deserving God's anger.

THALABI:v2p244/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p244/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه عن محمد بن إسحاق
THALABI:v2p244/r1.claim: After the king asked him to pray, Jeremiah asked God to spare Israel if righteous and destroy them if they persisted in wrongdoing; a heavenly lightning strike and ruined temple followed, and Jeremiah learned his own prayer had triggered it.

THALABI:v2p244/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p244/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p244/r2.claim: Nebuchadnezzar conquered Jerusalem, killed Israelites, destroyed the temple, selected one hundred thousand boys, and divided the rest among those left in Syria, taken captive, and killed; this was the first punishment for their injustice.

THALABI:v2p244/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p244/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p244/r3.claim: On returning to Jerusalem with grape juice and figs on his donkey, Jeremiah saw the ruins and asked how God would revive the town after its death.

THALABI:v2p244/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p244/r4.speaker: بعضهم
THALABI:v2p244/r4.claim: Those who say the traveler was Ezra place him among the Israelites deported to Babylon, alongside Daniel and seven thousand descendants of David.

THALABI:v2p245/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p245/r1.claim: Thaʿlabī identifies Ezra as the traveler who escaped Babylon, reached an abandoned village, ate its fruit and drank its grape juice, then wondered how God could revive it after death.

THALABI:v2p245/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r10.speaker: ابن محيصن والأعمش وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
THALABI:v2p245/r10.claim: These readers assimilate the thāʾ in labith and labithtum throughout the Qurʾan; the remaining readers pronounce it distinctly.

THALABI:v2p245/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p245/r2.claim: Ezra's question about reviving the village expressed amazement, not doubt in resurrection.

THALABI:v2p245/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r3.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p245/r3.claim: Wahb's account says Jeremiah tied his donkey, then God put him to sleep, took his soul for a hundred years, and killed the donkey while preserving its food and drink.

THALABI:v2p245/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r4.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p245/r4.claim: In Wahb's report, God concealed Jeremiah from sight and kept beasts and birds from eating his body.

THALABI:v2p245/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r5.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p245/r5.claim: After seventy years God ordered a king to rebuild Jerusalem and its surroundings; a thousand stewards each led three hundred thousand workers, and the city was rebuilt over thirty years.

THALABI:v2p245/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r6.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p245/r6.claim: Wahb's account says God destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito and returned surviving Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem.

THALABI:v2p245/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r7.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p245/r7.claim: At the hundred-year mark God revived Jeremiah's eyes and then body; he watched the donkey's scattered bones gather, receive flesh and skin, and revive.

THALABI:v2p245/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p245/r8.claim: Thaʿlabī says God restored Jeremiah to life; this is the event described by the verse's statement that God made him die for a hundred years and then raised him.

THALABI:v2p245/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p245/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p245/r9.claim: The interrogative kam asks for the amount of time he remained there.

THALABI:v2p246/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r1.claim: Assimilation is based on closeness of articulation and similarity in whispering; distinct pronunciation follows the written form. Both readings are eloquent, and labitha means to stay or reside.

THALABI:v2p246/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r10.speaker: الشاعر
THALABI:v2p246/r10.claim: A cited line uses al-taʿayyun as a witness for the relevant derivational pattern; the text explains that the poet intended that form.

THALABI:v2p246/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r11.speaker: العجاج
THALABI:v2p246/r11.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj's line is cited as an example of a form with an intended doubled letter, parallel to the word's derivation.

THALABI:v2p246/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r12.claim: The Arabic expression natalaʿā describes people going out to gather a tender plant called al-maqāʿ; the verse also cites daṣṣāhā for dassasahā.

THALABI:v2p246/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r13.claim: Readers who retain the hāʾ in both positions treat it as a root letter; on this account the word is sanhiyah, diminutive sunayhah, with the verb musāhanah.

THALABI:v2p246/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r2.claim: God caused him to die at midday and revived him a hundred years later near sunset, so he first thought a day had passed, then corrected himself to part of a day when he saw sunlight remaining.

THALABI:v2p246/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r3.claim: The particle aw signals a retraction from saying one day, as in the expression aw yazidun.

THALABI:v2p246/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r4.claim: The food was figs and the drink grape juice; they had not changed over the years.

THALABI:v2p246/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r5.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
THALABI:v2p246/r5.claim: Hamza and al-Kisāʾī omit the hāʾ of yat asannah in connected recitation, as they do in fa-bihudāhumuqtadih; the other readers retain it in pause and connection.

THALABI:v2p246/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r6.speaker: أبو حاتم عن طلحة
THALABI:v2p246/r6.claim: Abū Ḥātim reports Ṭalḥa's assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn and says this reading is also found in Ubayy's codex; the meaning is that years did not alter the food.

THALABI:v2p246/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r7.claim: One morphological analysis treats the hāʾ as an added pause-link: the original form is yasna, with yāʾ removed by jussive marking and hāʾ supplied at pause.

THALABI:v2p246/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p246/r8.claim: On the view that the hāʾ is added, sanah has a wāw root and plural sanawāt; its verb forms include sāniya and tasannā.

THALABI:v2p246/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p246/r9.speaker: أبو عمر
THALABI:v2p246/r9.claim: Abū ʿAmr derives the word from tasannun, meaning change, as in the description of altered mud as hamāʾ masnūn.

THALABI:v2p247/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p247/r1.claim: Although the verse mentions two items, the verb's change concerns the nearer word, the years; the other item is omitted as understood. Ibn Masʿūd's reading explicitly repeats the drink.

THALABI:v2p247/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p247/r10.claim: The rāʾ reading means that God revives the dead; Thaʿlabī links it to several Qurʾanic uses of nashara and nushūr.

THALABI:v2p247/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r11.speaker: حارثة بن بدر الغداني
THALABI:v2p247/r11.claim: Ḥāritha ibn Badr al-Ghadānī's verse uses anshara for reviving the dead and restoring their minds.

THALABI:v2p247/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v2p247/r2.claim: Ibn Masʿūd's reading says, “look at your food and this drink; it has not changed,” supporting the explanation of the singular verb.

THALABI:v2p247/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r3.speaker: أكثر العلماء
THALABI:v2p247/r3.claim: Most scholars take the verse as fronting and postponing its clauses: first look at the unchanged food and drink, then at the donkey; another possible reading leaves the sequence straightforward.

THALABI:v2p247/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r4.speaker: خارجة والأعرج وعيسى بن عمر وابن عامر وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
THALABI:v2p247/r4.claim: These readers incline the vowel in ḥimār and al-ḥimār; the remaining readers use the full, non-imālah pronunciation.

THALABI:v2p247/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r5.speaker: أبي بن كعب وعبد الله بن عامر والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
THALABI:v2p247/r5.claim: These readers pronounce nunshizuhā with zāy, a ḍamma on the nūn, and kasra on the shīn.

THALABI:v2p247/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r6.speaker: أبو العالية عن زيد بن ثابت
THALABI:v2p247/r6.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya reports Zayd ibn Thābit saying that the letter is actually rāʾ and readers merely dotted it as zāy; a parallel report from Ibn ʿAbbās is cited and Abū ʿUbayda prefers zāy.

THALABI:v2p247/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p247/r7.claim: The zāy reading means raising and moving the bones back to their bodily positions, assembling them together.

THALABI:v2p247/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r8.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
THALABI:v2p247/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī explain the verb as bringing the bones out; al-Kisāʾī explains it as making them grow and become large.

THALABI:v2p247/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p247/r9.speaker: قتادة وعطاء وأبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب وأيوب
THALABI:v2p247/r9.claim: These readers use nunshiru with rāʾ, meaning “revive”; Abū Ḥātim chooses this reading.

THALABI:v2p248/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r1.speaker: الحسن والمفضل
THALABI:v2p248/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Mufaḍḍal read nunshuruhā with rāʾ, fatḥa on nūn and ḍamma on shīn; al-Farrāʾ relates it to spreading and folding.

THALABI:v2p248/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p248/r2.claim: Some say this reading also means reviving; Abū Ḥātim says that usage is not familiar.

THALABI:v2p248/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r3.speaker: النخعي
THALABI:v2p248/r3.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī reads nunshizuhā with zāy and fatḥa on nūn; Abū Ḥātim calls it an error, while others treat nashazahu and anshazahu as synonymous.

THALABI:v2p248/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p248/r4.claim: “Then We cover them with flesh” compares covering the bones with flesh to covering a body with clothing.

THALABI:v2p248/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r5.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v2p248/r5.claim: Most commentators understand the bones to be the donkey's, which God had killed and then restored whole while the man watched.

THALABI:v2p248/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r6.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v2p248/r6.claim: Al-Suddī reports that God revived Ezra while the donkey's bones were scattered; a wind gathered and fitted them, flesh and blood covered them, and an angel blew into its nostrils so it rose and brayed.

THALABI:v2p248/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r7.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة والربيع وابن زيد
THALABI:v2p248/r7.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn Zayd say the bones are the man's: God revived his eyes while his body was dead, and his donkey remained alive as before.

THALABI:v2p248/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r8.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة والربيع وابن زيد
THALABI:v2p248/r8.claim: On this interpretation, the omitted phrase is “look at your bones”; the donkey stood as it had when tied, and its neck amulet remained new after a hundred years.

THALABI:v2p248/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p248/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p248/r9.claim: The phrase “and to make you a sign for people” explains the purpose of the event; the next segment develops its meaning.

THALABI:v2p249/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p249/r1.claim: A cited line by al-Aswad ibn Jaʿfar illustrates the interpretation of the conjunction as an extra wāw by using fa-idha dhalika to mean “when that happened.”

THALABI:v2p249/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r2.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v2p249/r2.claim: Most commentators say the event made him a sign, lesson, and proof of resurrection after death.

THALABI:v2p249/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r3.speaker: الضحاك وغيره
THALABI:v2p249/r3.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others say the sign was that he returned to his village young, with black hair and beard, while his children and grandchildren had become old.

THALABI:v2p249/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r4.speaker: قتادة عن كعب والحسن ومقاتل وجويبر عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس وعبد الله بن إسماعيل السدي عن أبيه عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p249/r4.claim: A report says the revived Ezra rode home, failed to recognize the village, and found his former blind, paralyzed servant, now 120, who asked him to restore her sight and mobility.

THALABI:v2p249/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
