THALABI:v2p249/r5.claim: In the report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ezra prayed and touched the woman's eyes; her sight and legs were restored and she recognized him.

THALABI:v2p249/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p249/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p249/r6.claim: The woman called the people together, including Ezra's aged son and grandsons; at first they disbelieved her claim that Ezra had returned.

THALABI:v2p250/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r1.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
THALABI:v2p250/r1.claim: These authorities say Ezra's son recognized him by a black, crescent-shaped mark between his shoulders.

THALABI:v2p250/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r2.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
THALABI:v2p250/r2.claim: They report that after Nebuchadnezzar burned the Torah, an angel gave Ezra water and God inscribed the Torah in his chest and sent him as a prophet.

THALABI:v2p250/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r3.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
THALABI:v2p250/r3.claim: Ezra dictated the Torah from memory; a man retrieved a copy buried in his grandfather's vineyard, and the two texts matched letter for letter.

THALABI:v2p250/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r4.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي والكلبي
THALABI:v2p250/r4.claim: They say the Israelites then called Ezra God's son because they thought no one could possess the Torah after its loss unless he were God's son.

THALABI:v2p250/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r5.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو رجاء وحمزة والكسائي
THALABI:v2p250/r5.claim: These readers connect qāla aʿlam as a jussive command, with God telling him “know”; ʿAbd Allāh and al-Aʿmash read qul aʿlam to support this.

THALABI:v2p250/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r6.speaker: الباقون
THALABI:v2p250/r6.claim: The remaining readers take qāla aʿlam as a declarative report that Ezra said he now knew God could do all things.

THALABI:v2p250/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p250/r7.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v2p250/r7.claim: Wahb reports that Paradise has no dogs or donkeys except the dog of the Cave Companions and Jeremiah's donkey.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r1.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r1.claim: Qatada identifies the passerby as Ezra; Wahb identifies him as Jeremiah; Ibn Ishaq identifies him as al-Khidr.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r10.claim: He learned that a century had passed from signs and reports and seeing his grandchildren as old people, though their fathers had been young men when he left.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r11.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r11.claim: Ali reports that Ezra left his pregnant wife at age fifty, returned from the hundred-year death at age fifty, and found his son a hundred years old, fifty years older than he was.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r12.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r12.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, and Abu Amr read nunshiruha with ra, meaning revive the bones; the dead are like something folded and revival unfolds them into action.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r13.speaker: الباقون
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r13.claim: The other readers pronounce nunshizuha with zay, meaning to raise the bones together; nushuz denotes elevation, as with raised land or a wife's rising from obedience.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r14.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r14.claim: It is said that God restored the man's eyes and sight before his body, so he watched the bones assemble, flesh cover them, and his donkey revive.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r15.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r15.claim: The one asking how long he had remained may have been an angel, a prophet, or an aged believer who witnessed his death and revival.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r2.speaker: وهب وقتادة والربيع بن أنس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r2.claim: Wahb, Qatada, and al-Rabi ibn Anas identify the village as Jerusalem after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it; Ibn Zayd says it was the village from which thousands fled fearing death.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r3.claim: Khawiya means ruined according to Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi, and al-Dahhak, or empty; its root denotes emptiness, also used for a house without inhabitants or a hungry belly.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r4.claim: Aruš means buildings or construction, so the village lay collapsed over its structures.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r5.claim: The question may ask how God will rebuild the ruined village or how He will restore its dead inhabitants.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r6.claim: He guessed he had been dead a day because he died early and awoke near the end of the day a century later, then revised his estimate on seeing the remaining sun.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r7.claim: The food and drink's failure to decay means they remained unchanged, from asin, water that has not changed; Ibn Zayd distinguishes it from ajin, changed but drinkable water.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r8.speaker: أبو عبيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r8.claim: Abu Ubayd says the food did not change because the years had not passed over it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p331/r9.claim: It is said his food was juice, figs, and grapes; the juice was sweet and the fruit remained fresh.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r1.claim: The verse is semantically coordinated with the preceding one: “Have you seen the one who disputed, or the one who passed by?” Arabs often coordinate by meaning, as the cited poems show.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r2.claim: He instead treats the كاف as extra and coordinates الذي with the earlier الذي in the verse about the disputant.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r3.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r3.claim: He chooses semantic coordination as a good grammatical account.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r4.speaker: قتادة والربيع وعكرمة والضحاك والسدي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r4.claim: They identify the person who passed by the ruined town as ʿUzayr.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r5.speaker: وهب وعطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r5.claim: They identify the passerby as Armiya, also described in the segment as al-Khidr.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p378#2/r6.claim: He says the passerby was an unbelieving man who doubted resurrection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r1.speaker: وهب وعكرمة وقتادة والربيع
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r1.claim: They identify the town as Iliya, Jerusalem.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r2.claim: He identifies it as the town from which the multitudes fled fearing death, mentioned in 2:243.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r3.claim: Khāwi means empty or vacant; the root also describes an empty belly, gaps between a horse's legs, and open land, while a ruined house is vacant of inhabitants and fallen stars or rainless clouds are empty of rain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r4.claim: The poem by Abu al-Najm uses خواء for the space a horse's long stride leaves across the ground.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p380/r5.claim: ʿArsh means a house roof; ʿurush are wooden structures or ceilings, and the verb describes building with wood.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والربيع والضحاك
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r1.claim: They explain the town as ruined and collapsed: walls remained, roofs fell, then the walls toppled from their foundations onto the roofs.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r2.claim: Khāwi can mean uprooted; 69:7 and 54:20 describe palm stumps as uprooted, making this an especially vivid description of ruined houses.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r3.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r3.claim: An uprooted wall leaves an empty place, so a house is called khāwi after its wall collapses.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r4.speaker: بعضهم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p382/r4.claim: They take على عروشها to mean empty of its roofs, with على used in the sense of عن, as in 83:2.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r1.claim: A year covers a winter and a summer; some derive it from swimming because it allows a long course of activity.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r2.claim: The food is figs and the drink is juice.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r3.speaker: ابن عباس في رواية عطاء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r3.claim: لم يتسنه means the food did not change or rot over one hundred years; Abu ʿUbayda similarly says the years did not alter it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r4.claim: There are two readings, retaining or dropping the هاء in connected speech; it is retained at a pause in either case.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r5.claim: The root of سنة may be سنوة or سنهة; forms such as أسنت القوم, سنوات, and سانيت support سنوة, as does Labid's verse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r6.claim: With the هاء omitted, he explains the word from التسني, change over time, on the سنوة derivation: the food and drink did not change as juice ordinarily would.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r7.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r7.claim: He allows سنة to derive from سننه, citing the diminutive سنينة; لم يتسن could then come from لم يتسنن, with a نون changed to ياء because of repeated nūns.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r8.speaker: الفراء وأبو عمرو الشيباني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p386/r8.claim: They also derive the form without هاء from مسنون, meaning changed, with نون replaced by ياء.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r1.claim: A cited verse naming two animal parts but predicating of one supports the construction; Ibn Masʿud's reading explicitly separates the food and drink and says the drink did not change.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r2.claim: The donkey's bones decayed while the food and drink stayed unchanged; God then reassembled its limbs in order, restored it to life, and it stood braying at the man's head.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r3.speaker: بعضهم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r3.claim: They treat the واو in ولنجعلك as extra, with its لام governed by لبثت: God made him die and revived him for a hundred years to make him a sign.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r4.claim: He says the واو introduces an implied verb: God did this to make the man a sign, like the implied verbs in 6:105 and 6:75.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r5.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r5.claim: The man became a sign because his revival after death demonstrated resurrection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r6.speaker: الضحاك وغيره
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p392/r6.claim: They say God made him a sign by reviving him young, with dark hair and beard, while his grandsons were gray-haired.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r1.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r1.claim: They take “the bones” to mean the donkey's bones; the definite article substitutes for a possessive pronoun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r2.speaker: قتادة والربيع وابن زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r2.claim: They say the bones are the man's: God revived his eyes and head while the rest of his body was dead, but his donkey had remained standing, alive, without food or water for a century.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r3.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r3.claim: He says the verse means both the man's bones and the donkey's bones.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r4.claim: On the reading ننشرها, the verb means revive or raise the dead; 80:22 and 36:78–79 also describe the dead being raised or bones revived.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r5.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r5.claim: The reading ننشرها with fatḥa on نون and ḍamma on شين suggests spreading after folding: living movement unfolds the body that was folded in death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r6.claim: Others treat نشر and أنشر as intransitive and causative pairs, as in حسرت الدابة/حسرتها and غاض الماء/غضته; al-ʿAjjaj's camel verse illustrates this usage.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r7.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r7.claim: They read ننشزها with زاي, meaning raise the bones and fit some to others; this is the sense of restoring them to their places and joining them together.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p394/r8.claim: The root نشز means rise or stand apart; a wife's نشوز is her resisting ordinary married conduct and rising above the husband's satisfaction.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r1.speaker: الأخفش
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r1.claim: Both نشزته and أنشزته can mean “I raised it.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r2.speaker: النخعي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r2.claim: He reportedly read ننشزها with fatḥa on نون and ḍamma on شين and زاي.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r3.claim: After witnessing God revive him, the man knew God's power in a newly certain, direct way, having seen what he had previously known only as unseen.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r4.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r4.claim: They read قال اعلم as an imperative addressed by the man to himself, treating himself rhetorically like a separate interlocutor; al-Aʿsha gives a similar self-address.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p396/r5.claim: Alternatively, God may have told him “Know”; the reading قيل اعلم reported from ʿAbd Allah and al-Aʿmash supports that interpretation.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r1.claim: The passerby was ʿUzayr, and the ruined town was Iliya; its buildings had collapsed over their roofs.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r2.claim: ʿUzayr wondered how God could restore the town after its destruction, so God chose to show resurrection through him.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r3.claim: He arrived on a donkey carrying a small vessel of juice and a basket of figs; God put him to sleep, took his soul for a century, then revived him.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r4.claim: His food and drink remained unchanged for a hundred years as evidence of the elapsed time, while his donkey lay dead with visible bones.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r5.claim: The wāw in “so We may make you a sign” is extra; he was a sign because he returned youthful with black hair while his grandsons were gray.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r6.claim: “Nunshizuhā” means reviving the bones; another reading, “nunshizuhā,” means raising them from the ground, since elevation is called nushūz.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:259-260/r7.claim: After seeing the donkey reassembled and clothed with flesh, ʿUzayr knew by direct observation what he had previously known only unseen.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r1.claim: The verse continues the preceding account of Abraham's disputant; another reading treats it as a separate question asking whether one has seen both men.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r2.speaker: قتادة، عكرمة، الضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r2.claim: Qatada, Ikrima, and al-Dahhak identify the passerby as Uzayr ibn Sharhiya.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r3.claim: Wahb identifies him as Armiya ibn Hilqiya, from Aaron's tribe, and says he was al-Khidr.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r4.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r4.claim: Mujahid says the passerby was an unbeliever who doubted resurrection.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r5.claim: Reported locations for the village include Jerusalem, the holy land, Dayr Sabir Abad, Muslim Badh, Dayr Hiraql, a village destroyed with its fleeing inhabitants, and an "grape village" two farsakhs from Jerusalem.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r6.claim: Khawiya can describe a fallen or an empty house; the village lay collapsed on its roofs, with roofs falling first and walls then falling onto them.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p317/r7.claim: Arush means roofs, though it can also refer to any structure; the image describes the walls falling over the collapsed roofs.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r1.claim: The Hijaz and Basra readers read nunsiruha with an r, meaning revive the bones; others read nunshizuha with a z, meaning raise and reassemble them.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r2.speaker: السدي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r2.claim: Most exegetes take the bones as the donkey's; al-Suddi describes winds gathering the scattered bones, God assembling them, then covering them with flesh before an angel revives the animal.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r3.claim: Another group says God did not kill the donkey but killed the man, restoring his eyes and head while his body remained dead; the donkey remained intact, so the text's order is inverted.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r4.speaker: قتادة عن كعب، والضحاك عن ابن عباس، والسدي عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320#2/r4.claim: They narrate that Uzayr returned to find an ancient blind, lame woman who had known him; at his prayer she regained sight and mobility, recognized him, and summoned his son and descendants, who identified his birthmark.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r1.claim: After the village's restoration, a call ordered the dead man to live; he rose and his donkey brayed, and God preserved Armiya's life in the wilderness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r10.speaker: الضحاك وغيره
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r10.claim: Al-Dahhak and others say he returned to his village as a young man, while his descendants were elderly and his hair remained black.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r2.claim: He thought he had been dead a day because he died at midmorning and awoke late in the day a century later, before sunset.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r3.claim: The preserved food was figs and the drink was juice; they appeared freshly picked and pressed despite the century.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r4.speaker: الكسائي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r4.claim: Al-Kisa'i explains lam yatasannah as though years had not passed over it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r5.claim: Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Yaqub omit the h in connected recitation; others retain it. The omitted h may be an added pause marker after an original yatasanna.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r6.speaker: أبو عمرو
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r6.claim: Abu Amr derives yatasannah from a two-nun form meaning to change, as in the description of altered mud; the author also reports a view that the h is original to the word for year.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r7.claim: The singular verb for the unspoiled food and drink refers to the nearer noun, drink, and suffices because both share the meaning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r8.claim: When the man looked at the donkey, its bones were white; God joined them, clothed them with flesh and skin, and revived it before his eyes.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r9.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p320/r9.claim: The waw in 'and to make you a sign' may be superfluous; al-Farra says it signals a condition for a following act, with the sense 'to make you a sign of resurrection.'

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r1.speaker: السدي والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r1.claim: Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi say Nebuchadnezzar had burned the Torah; an angel gave Uzayr water that imprinted the Torah in his chest, and he recited it to Israel, who then called him God's son.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r2.claim: The story of Israel's calling Uzayr God's son is deferred to the account in Surat al-Tawbah.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p321/r3.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'know' as a connected jussive command from God to Uzayr; others read it as Uzayr's declarative statement after seeing the resurrection.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r7.claim: The phrase أو كالذي means ‘or did you see one like him’; أرأيت is omitted because ألم تر already signals the exclamatory construction.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r8.claim: By sense, it may mean ‘or like the one who disputed Abraham,’ or ‘or like the passerby’; the latter was apparently an unbeliever, in parallel with Nimrod and the expression of incredulity.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r9.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p333/r9.claim: Another view identifies the passerby as Ezra or al-Khidr, who wanted to witness resurrection and increase his certainty, like Abraham.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r1.claim: The passerby's question ‘how?’ acknowledges that he cannot know the manner of revival and magnifies the reviver's power.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r2.claim: The ruined village is Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it; another view identifies it as the village from which thousands departed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r3.claim: He estimated that a day or part of one had passed because he died in the morning and was raised a century later before sunset; seeing the remaining sun corrected his estimate.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r4.claim: A report says his food was figs and grapes and his drink juice or milk; the fruit seemed freshly picked and the drink unchanged.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r5.claim: لم يتسنه means the food did not change; its final ه may be a root letter or pause suffix, with an etymology from year because things change over time.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r6.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p334/r6.claim: An alternative derives the word from putrid mud, with one n assimilated into a weak letter.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r1.claim: The bones may be the donkey's bones or those of the dead whose revival had amazed the passerby.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r2.claim: The reading ننشزها means reassembling by moving and raising bones into place; al-Hasan's ننشرها derives from God's raising the dead.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r3.claim: The subject of تبين is omitted and understood as ‘that God is powerful over all things,’ indicated by the following statement; alternatively, what became clear was resurrection itself.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas read فلما تبين له in the passive voice; another reading has an imperative ‘know,’ while Abdullah's reading has ‘it was said: know.’

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335#2/r5.claim: If the passerby had been an unbeliever, God could address him after raising him, when he was no longer an unbeliever.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r1.claim: The food had not aged through the century and remained as it was, as though a hundred years had not passed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r2.speaker: عبد الله
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r2.claim: Abdullah's reading has ‘this is your drink’ and omits the final h in لم يتسن.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r3.speaker: أبي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r3.claim: Ubayy read لم يسنه, assimilating the tāʾ into the sīn.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r4.claim: The donkey's bones had scattered and decayed; alternatively, it remained alive where tied for a century without food or water, like the preserved food and drink.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p335/r5.claim: One account says Ezra returned on his donkey and recited the Torah from memory while the people checked it, prompting them to call him God's son; another says his children had aged while he remained young.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r1.claim: “Or” connects by meaning to the rhetorical question “Have you not seen the one who argued,” whose sense is “Have you seen one like this?”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r10.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r10.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the town with the place of the thousands who fled their homes fearing death, as in 2:243; al-Ṭabarī titled the story accordingly.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Ibn Zayd’s identification: the verse points to the town itself and its desolation, whereas his account points to bones and bodies, not a deserted built-up town.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r12.speaker: وهب بن منبه وقتادة والضحاك وعكرمة والربيع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r12.claim: They identify the town as Jerusalem, ruined by the Babylonian Nebuchadnezzar after Israelite wrongdoing.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r2.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حسين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r2.claim: He reads the waw of “or” with fatḥa, treating it as a conjunction preceded by the interrogative hamza.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r3.speaker: سليمان بن بريدة وناجية بن كعب وقتادة وابن عباس والربيع وعكرمة والضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r3.claim: They identify the man who passed the town as ʿUzayr.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير وبكر بن مضر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r4.claim: They identify the man as Jeremiah.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r5.speaker: ابن إسحاق
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r5.claim: Ibn Isḥāq identifies Jeremiah with al-Khiḍr, a claim al-Naqqāsh also transmits from Wahb.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds that identification implausible: al-Khiḍr was contemporary with Moses, whereas this man lived later, though perhaps the names coincided.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r7.claim: Mujāhid says the man was an unnamed Israelite.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r8.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r8.claim: Al-Naqqāsh also transmits the claim that the man was Lot’s servant-boy.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r9.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p347/r9.claim: Al-Naqqāsh reports that some identify the town as al-Muʾtafikah.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r1.speaker: ابن جريج وقتادة والربيع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r1.claim: They say the man died in the morning and was raised before sunset; seeing the remaining sunlight, he first guessed a day and then qualified it as part of a day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r10.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r10.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads “this is your food and drink; it has not changed.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r11.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r11.claim: They read “look at your food and drink for a hundred years.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r12.claim: Readers differ over retaining the hāʾ in the connected pronunciation of several Qur’anic words; they all retain it at pauses, with Ḥamza deleting these forms in connected reading and al-Kisāʾī deleting it in two forms.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r2.claim: He was told that he had been dead for a hundred years and inferred this from the town’s new buildings and trees.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r3.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r3.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives the word for year from a sun’s circuit through its orbit, using swimming as a metaphor.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r4.claim: The apparent sense is that death occurred through the soul’s departure from the body.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r5.claim: A story says a king was sent to rebuild the town until it was complete when the speaker was raised.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r6.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم ونافع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r6.claim: They pronounce the final consonants distinctly in labithtu throughout the Qur’an because thāʾ and tāʾ have different articulation points.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r7.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r7.claim: They assimilate the two consonants throughout the Qur’an, treating them alike because both are articulated at the tongue tip and upper teeth and are voiceless.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r8.speaker: أبو علي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r8.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the assimilation is supported by the two consonants’ occurrence together in a single rhyme.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348#2/r9.claim: One interpretation is that the food and drink remained unchanged and the donkey stayed alive; another makes the donkey itself the spectacle of resurrection.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r1.claim: An ʿarsh is a roof or any structure made for shade; the verse at 16:68 uses the same verb for what bees build.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r10.claim: A narrative says Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and exiled Israel; Jeremiah returned to see the ruin, then God caused him to die for a hundred years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r11.claim: Versions differ over whether the man was Jeremiah or ʿUzayr, whether his donkey survived or decomposed, and what his food and drink consisted of; some say donkey and man both decomposed, others only one did.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r12.claim: One account says God restored the city and returned Israelites there by the hundredth year; another says the man saw thirty years of rebuilding after seventy years dead, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak against the verse’s wording.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r13.claim: “Then He raised him” means God gave him life and movement; God questioned him through an angel, and “how long” is an adverb of time.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r2.claim: Al-Suddī understands the houses to have collapsed so that their roofs fell first and walls fell on top of them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r3.speaker: غير السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r3.claim: Others say the place was empty of people, while its houses and roofs remained standing.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r4.claim: The use of ʿarsh with “upon” is also found in the report describing the mosque’s roof on the Night of Decree.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r5.claim: Khawiya means empty or deserted; al-Ṭabarī regards the form khawat as the more eloquent.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r6.claim: “How will God bring this back to life?” literally asks by what means the city could be restored and repopulated; it may express grief for a lost home and its people.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r7.claim: Another possible meaning is a question about resurrecting the dead from among its former inhabitants.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r8.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r8.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits a view that the speaker doubted God’s power to resurrect, which prompted the personal demonstration.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p348/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says there is no doubt about God’s ability to rebuild a town, and the verse should not be interpreted as expressing doubt about resurrection either.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r1.claim: A poem illustrates the form in which hāʾ is part of the word for year; under this dialect the connected form must retain hāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r10.claim: The entire death and revival is a sign for all generations; no need exists to single out one aspect of it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r11.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r11.claim: They read the bones as “We bring them to life” with ḍamma on the first nūn and rāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r12.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r12.claim: They read the bones with zāy, “We raise them.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r13.speaker: أبان عن عاصم وابن عباس والحسن وأبو حيوة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r13.claim: They are reported to read the verb with initial nūn fatḥa, shin ḍamma, and rāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r2.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r2.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif reads the form with assimilation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r3.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r3.claim: Al-Naqqāsh connects “has not changed” with “water that is not stale” in 47:15; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes grammarians reject the derivation because the expected form would be different.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r4.claim: They say “look at your donkey” means watching its bones rejoin and its body come to life piece by piece; one version has an angel breathe life into it after it is reassembled.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r5.speaker: الضحاك ووهب بن منبه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r5.claim: They instead say the donkey remained alive and tethered for the whole hundred years, and the bones to be watched were the man’s own; people’s sight was veiled from them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says storytellers multiplied details about this event, which he abbreviates because they are not sound.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r7.speaker: الأعمش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r7.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the man became a sign because he returned young as on the day of his death, while his descendants had aged.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r8.speaker: عكرمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r8.claim: ʿIkrima says he returned at age forty, as when he died, while his sons had passed one hundred.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r9.speaker: غير الأعمش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p349/r9.claim: Others say he was a sign because everyone he had known had died, so his story was known by the surviving community through reports.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r1.claim: The reading nunshiruhā with rāʾ means “We revive them,” as in the verse about God raising the dead and in al-Aʿshā’s poem.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r10.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r10.claim: The same reading is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb is reported to read the verb with yāʾ and shin.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r11.claim: Kiswah is clothing that covers; meat is metaphorically likened to it, as in al-Nābigha’s poem comparing Islam to a garment.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r2.speaker: الأعشى
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r2.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s line about a dead man rising is cited as evidence for the verb meaning revival.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r3.claim: The reading with initial fatḥa may be a dialect variant meaning revive, or may mean spread out the bones after death folded them together.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r4.claim: The zāy reading means raising the bones; Abū ʿAlī and others interpret it as raising each bone toward another for revival.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r5.claim: A poem about a fox atop a rise illustrates the root’s sense of elevation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r6.speaker: الأعشى
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r6.claim: Al-Aʿshā uses nāshizan for a woman rising or standing apart, another example of the root.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya is uneasy with the sense of bones being raised toward one another: nushūz usually means slight elevation, so he envisages the growth of decayed bone fragments through creation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r8.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r8.claim: Al-Naqqāsh glosses nunshizuhā as making the bones grow; usages for a camel’s tooth, rising, and a woman’s altered state support gradual elevation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r9.speaker: النخعي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p350/r9.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī reads the verb with fatḥa on initial nūn, ḍamma on shin, and zāy.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r1.claim: A report describes flesh, sinews, and veins joining and connecting before the donkey was complete.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r10.speaker: أبو علي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r10.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the reading can mean knowledge of a kind he had not previously known, namely direct experiential knowledge, in Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s clarification.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r11.claim: The imperative reading could be the angel addressing him, or the speaker addressing himself as a separate person; Abū ʿAlī cites poems with this self-address construction.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r2.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r2.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says “when it became clear to him” means he saw with his eyes what he had doubted God could do.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects al-Ṭabarī’s gloss as forcing an implication unsupported by the wording and relying on an anomalous, weak possibility.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r4.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r4.claim: They read “I know that God is powerful” with a separated hamza and ḍamma on mīm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r5.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r5.claim: They read “he said, Know that God is powerful” with a connected hamza and sukūn on mīm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r6.speaker: أبو رجاء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r6.claim: Abū Rajāʾ is also reported to use the imperative reading.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود والأعمش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r7.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and al-Aʿmash read “it was said, Know.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r8.claim: The passive reading plainly means an angel told him to know; the first reading plainly means he himself concluded that God can do all things.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p351/r9.claim: He rejects the implication that the speaker was previously denying resurrection; rather, reflection prompts a believer to affirm God’s power, as when seeing a marvel.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r1.speaker: أبو الحسن
TABRISI:2:259#2/r1.claim: The imperative reading اعلم addresses the speaker himself after he witnessed the resurrection, as poets sometimes address themselves in the second person; Abu al-Hasan says it fits best.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r10.claim: كم is the object of لبثت; the waw in ولنجعلك joins a suppressed verb, and كيف can modify the revival or the bones' state.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r2.speaker: الأعشى
TABRISI:2:259#2/r2.claim: Al-A'sha's line أنت بين القرو والعاصر addresses the poet himself as أنت, illustrating self-address in the imperative reading.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r3.claim: خاوية means empty; a village is named for gathering residents, and خاوية على عروشها can mean its walls remain without roofs or that it lies fallen over its buildings.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABRISI:2:259#2/r4.claim: Abu Ubayda interprets عروش as tents, the dwellings of nomads; another lexical view explains them as roofs or buildings.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r5.claim: أنى asks from where or how; a year is a full cycle after winter and summer, while swimming and the verb لبث denote movement through water and remaining in place.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r6.claim: The word حمار covers both domestic and wild asses; نشر is the opposite of folding and can also mean spreading news, scent, or a healing charm.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r7.claim: The initial kaf coordinates the scene with Abraham's dispute; its syntactic position is accusative, and the passage expresses amazement because it exceeds ordinary cases.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r8.claim: The kaf may instead be emphatic extra wording, but the author prefers the first parsing because extra particles should not be posited without necessity.

TABRISI:2:259#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#2/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#2/r9.claim: أنى is a question about the manner or kind of revival, not a denial that revival can occur; it may parse as a circumstantial accusative or verbal noun.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r1.claim: لم يتسنه means the food and drink were not altered by years; masculine singular can denote the generic food and drink, or the referent may be the nearer drink alone.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r10.claim: أعلم means I know with certainty; the imperative reading is self-address or an order from God. He was not doubtful before, but witnessing made inferential knowledge immediate and certain.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r2.claim: Another account says the provisions were juice, figs, and grapes, unusually susceptible to spoiling, yet remained as freshly gathered.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r3.claim: The donkey's scattered bones demonstrate how long the man had been dead; he is asked to observe their restoration and the animal's revival.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r4.claim: The bones may be those of the donkey, according to al-Suddi and others, or the man's bones, according to al-Dahhak, Qatada, and al-Rabi'.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r5.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة والربيع
TABRISI:2:259#3/r5.claim: Al-Dahhak, Qatada, and al-Rabi' say the man's bones were revived; first his eye returned like the thin film on an egg, then scattered bones and meat reassembled until he and the donkey stood.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r6.claim: God made him a sign for people as a proof of resurrection, either in answer to his request or through what happened to him and his donkey.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r7.claim: He learned the century had passed from God's miraculous signs in his body, food, drink, and donkey, and from worldly changes he saw on returning home.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r8.speaker: علي
TABRISI:2:259#3/r8.claim: Ali reports that Uzayr left at fifty with a pregnant wife, died for a century, and returned still fifty while his son was a hundred years old.

TABRISI:2:259#3/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259#3/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259#3/r9.claim: Another report says Nebuchadnezzar burned the Torah; Uzayr recited it from memory and produced a copy hidden in his grandfather's vineyard, matching it exactly, after which they said he was God's son.

TABRISI:2:259/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r1.claim: Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate the final sounds in لبثت; the remaining readers pronounce them separately.

TABRISI:2:259/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r2.claim: Iraqi readers except Abu Amr and Asim omit the h in لم يتسن when continuing; others retain it in continuation, and all retain it at pause.

TABRISI:2:259/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r3.claim: Hijaz and Basra read ننشرها with shin and ra for reviving; Kufa and Syria read ننشزها with zay for raising; Aban from Asim has a rare ra reading.

TABRISI:2:259/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r4.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i join the alif in قال اعلم and read a command; others separate it and read a declarative statement.

TABRISI:2:259/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r5.speaker: أبو علي
TABRISI:2:259/r5.claim: Abu Ali explains assimilation by shared tongue-tip articulation and voicelessness; non-assimilation reflects the letters' different articulation groups.

TABRISI:2:259/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r6.claim: With h in لم يتسنه, possible accounts derive it from sanah as a root or from year-related forms, or connect the word to change as in المسنون; on pause-marker analyses h drops in connected speech.

TABRISI:2:259/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r7.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
TABRISI:2:259/r7.claim: Abu Amr al-Shaybani is reported to derive the form from something changed or altered, comparing the change with a form in which sounds were transposed.

TABRISI:2:259/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r8.claim: The h in اقتده may stand for the implied verbal noun, following the verb's meaning, rather than be a pausal h; the parallel is the source pronoun in 3:180.

TABRISI:2:259/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:259/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:259/r9.claim: In the verse, ننشرها means revive the bones; ننشزها means raise and fit them together, with نشوز also used when a wife withdraws from marital relations.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r1.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r1.claim: The clause connects with the preceding question, meaning: consider the one who argued with Abraham, or the one who passed by a town.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r2.speaker: وهب وقتادة والربيع بن أنس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r2.claim: The ruined town was Jerusalem, after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r3.claim: The town was the one from which thousands had fled, fearing death.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وأبو العالية وعكرمة وسعيد بن جبير وناجية بن كعب وقتادة والضحاك والسدي ومقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r4.claim: The passerby was the prophet Uzayr, according to these authorities.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r5.speaker: وهب ومجاهد وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r5.claim: The passerby was Armiya, according to these authorities.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r6.claim: Another report from Mujahid identifies the passerby as an unbeliever who doubted resurrection.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r7.claim: Khawiya means empty; Ibn Qutayba glosses it as ruin, and urush are roofs that fall first, followed by the walls.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p308#2/r8.claim: If the passerby was a prophet, he wanted to see how resurrection occurs or to marvel at God's power; if an unbeliever, he was doubting. The prophetic interpretation is stronger.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r1.speaker: ناجية بن كعب عن علي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r1.claim: Ali's report says Uzayr, a young prophet, passed the ruined town; God revived him after a century, first creating his eyes so he watched his bones assemble, then receive flesh and spirit.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r2.claim: God took the passerby at the beginning of a day and raised him at its end, a hundred years later.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r3.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r3.claim: A voice from heaven asked how long he had stayed; he answered a day or part of one.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r4.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r4.claim: He first said a day, then seeing some sun remaining, corrected himself to “or part of a day.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r5.claim: Wahb's account identifies the traveler as Armiya: after seeing ruined Jerusalem with a donkey, figs, grapes, and water, he died; God began rebuilding the city seventy years later, revived his eyes to witness it, then restored his spirit and body after thirty more years while his food and donkey remained unchanged.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r6.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p309/r6.claim: Muqatil dates this story to after Jesus was raised.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r1.claim: These readers pronounce the th in لبثت distinctly; Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r2.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r2.claim: Distinct pronunciation preserves the two different articulation regions; assimilation treats the sounds as near enough in place and both voiceless.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r3.speaker: وهب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r3.claim: The traveler carried figs, grapes, and water in a small container.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p310/r4.claim: The traveler had figs and grapes with juice that never soured or fermented.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r1.claim: The lām in “to make you a sign” attaches to an omitted verb: God did this to show His power and make the man a sign for people.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r2.claim: Uzayr was forty and his son twenty when he died; after the resurrection Uzayr was forty and his son was 120, and Uzayr returned to Jerusalem and dictated its lost Torah to people who could no longer recite it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r3.claim: The bones God raised may have been the man's, the donkey's, or both.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r4.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r4.claim: They read ننشرها, meaning “revive them”; the related verb means God revives the dead.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r5.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r5.claim: They read ننشزها from elevation, meaning that God raises the bones together for revival; al-A'mash has a related variant.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r6.speaker: الحسن وأبان عن عاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311#2/r6.claim: They read ننشرها with an open initial nūn, comparing resurrection to unfolding what death had folded.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r1.claim: These readers retain the hāʾ in وصل for يتسنه and four other forms; Hamza deletes it in وصل, and al-Kisa'i does so for يتسنه and اقتده; all retain it at pause.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r2.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r2.claim: Lam yatasannah means the food and drink did not change.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r3.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r3.claim: It means unchanged through the passing years; the word relates to a palm tree bearing one year and resting the next.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r4.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p311/r4.claim: The donkey's bones had turned white and its joints separated, but God restored it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r1.claim: When it became clear to him, he saw the resurrection of the dead.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r2.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r2.claim: They read أَعْلَمُ as a declarative: “I now know by witnessing what I previously knew unseen.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r3.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r3.claim: They read اعلم as an imperative, apparently God's command; Abu Ali says the man addresses himself as another person.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r4.speaker: الجعفي عن أبي بكر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p312/r4.claim: A further reading has a kasra on the lām and is an imperative directing him to inform someone else.

RAZI-FULL:v7p19/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p19/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p19/r1.claim: The passage presents three stories: the first establishes the Creator, the second establishes resurrection, and the first is Abraham's debate with his contemporary ruler.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r1.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو علي الفارسي وأكثر النحويين
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r1.claim: The preceding ألم تر is understood as ألم تر كالذي, so أو كالذي is coordinated by meaning: Have you considered the one who disputed Abraham, or the one who passed a town.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r2.speaker: الأخفش
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the kaf in أو كالذي as extra, yielding the sense ألم تر إلى الذي حاج والذي مر على قرية.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r3.speaker: المبرد
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r3.claim: Al-Mubarrad supplies an omitted phrase: Have you considered the one who disputed Abraham and someone like the one who passed a town.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r4.speaker: مجاهد وأكثر المفسرين من المعتزلة
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r4.claim: One reported view identifies the passer as an unbeliever who doubted resurrection.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r5.speaker: قتادة وعكرمة والضحاك والسدي
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r5.claim: Those commentators identify the passer, whom they regard as a believer, as Ezra (Uzayr).

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r6.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r6.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through Ata identifies the passer as Jeremiah; some identify Jeremiah with al-Khidr, while Muhammad ibn Ishaq calls him a man of Aaron's tribe.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r7.speaker: وهب بن منبه
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r7.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah was the prophet God sent when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and burned the Torah.

RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p25/r8.claim: An argument for identifying the passer as an unbeliever is that his question sounds like someone who deems God's revival after death unlikely, which would be unbelief.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r1.claim: A second argument for the passer's prophethood is that God directly asks how long he stayed, tells him the duration, and commands him to inspect the bones; the wording gives no basis to insert an angel or messenger.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r2.claim: The suggestion that an angel or messenger relayed God's words departs from the apparent wording without evidence, so al-Razi rejects it.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r3.claim: A third argument says that reviving the man, preserving his food and drink, and restoring his donkey are great honors unsuitable for an unbeliever.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r4.claim: The proposal that these wonders honored another prophet fails because the passage gives no mention or sign of such a prophet, though supporting that prophet would be the story's main point.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26#2/r5.claim: Al-Razi answers that extraordinary signs may appear through someone whom God knows will later become a messenger, resolving the objection that the miracle preceded any prophetic claim.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r1.claim: The objection that the passer could have been prepubescent fails because God would not present a child's doubt as astonishing; al-Razi counters that the question may express ordinary improbability, not doubt in divine power.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r2.claim: The unbelief argument from فلما تبين له is weak: visible resurrection had not yet been shown, but that does not prove he lacked prior inferential knowledge.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r3.claim: The claim that أعلم proves he learned God's power only then is weak; the witnessed event added certainty and reassurance without showing that he lacked the underlying knowledge earlier.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r4.claim: The argument that the passer was grouped with Nimrod is weak because Abraham's question about resurrection follows this story, making it fitting that the passer was a prophet like Abraham.

RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p26/r5.claim: The believer-prophet view argues that his question presupposes knowledge of God and of resurrection in principle, since singling out this case as astonishing makes sense only if resurrection is generally possible.

RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r1.claim: A fourth argument treats ولنجعلك آية للناس as prophetic language, linked to 21:91; even if it does not explicitly confer prophethood, it promises great honor unsuitable for an unbeliever.

RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r2.claim: The alternative that the passer himself became a public sign through his unchanged youth is rejected: the wording promises to make him a sign after his revival, so it must mean more than the revival already witnessed.

RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p27/r3.claim: Al-Razi's second reply is that being made a sign entails great honor, which does not suit someone who died in unbelief and doubt about God's power.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r1.speaker: وهب وقتادة وعكرمة والربيع
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r1.claim: Wahb, Qatada, Ikrima, and al-Rabi identify the town as Jerusalem; Ibn Zayd instead identifies the town from which thousands fled fearing death.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r2.speaker: الأصمعي
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r2.claim: Al-Asma'i explains khāwiyat as empty of inhabitants, with related uses for an empty belly, the Prophet's posture in prostration, a horse's stance, and stars setting without rain; ʿarsh is a roof or wooden building.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas's description has the walls standing after the roofs collapsed, then the walls uprooted and falling onto the ruined roofs; the ruin is likened to uprooted palm stumps.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r4.claim: One reading takes على as عن, so the town is empty of its roofs, as in the expression about taking from people.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r5.claim: Another reading says the town was ruined while its fruit trellises remained; that contrast makes the ruin more astonishing because such structures normally disappear in an empty town.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r6.claim: The passer's question means how or when God will restore the town; if he was a disbeliever it expresses doubt, while a prophet may mean customary improbability or request further confirmation, like Abraham.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p28#2/r7.claim: Here i.e. annā means from where or when; reviving the town means rebuilding it, as if he thought restoration would not occur, so God showed him a sign in his own person.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas's occasion report says Nebuchadnezzar captured Israelites, including the scholar Ezra, who entered an abandoned town, wondered about its restoration by customary improbability, ate figs and grapes, drank juice, and slept.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r2.claim: In the report, God caused Ezra to die for a hundred years while young, concealed the death from people and animals, then revived him and asked how long he had remained dead.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r3.claim: The report says Ezra saw unchanged figs, grapes, and drink, then his donkey's bones gathered, were reassembled, clothed with flesh and skin, and restored to life; Ezra prostrated and acknowledged God's power.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r4.claim: After a century, Jerusalem's people recognized Ezra as the man their fathers said had died in Babylon; he recited the Torah from memory, and it matched the recovered copy, prompting them to call him God's son.

RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p28/r5.claim: Al-Razi says the widely circulated report supports identifying the passer as a prophet.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r1.claim: A hundred-year interval, rather than one day, makes revival more remote to reason and makes the changes he and others witness more astonishing.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r2.claim: Baʿath means bringing him back to life; the Resurrection is named the Day of Baʿth, from raising a she-camel, and this wording indicates he returned as the same rational person prepared to reason about divine knowledge.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r3.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate the consonants in كم لبثت; the remaining readers pronounce them distinctly, respectively because the articulations are close or distinct.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r4.claim: All agree that God is the speaker of كم لبثت; the miraculous context and the passer's later sight of the donkey and decayed bones identify the speaker as God.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r5.claim: God's question does not seek information; it alerts the passer to the extraordinary events that have occurred.

RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p29/r6.claim: He says a day or part of one because duration felt the same to a dead person, so he gave the shortest certain estimate; he died early in the day and then saw sunlight still remaining.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r1.speaker: كثير من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r1.claim: Many derive سنة from سنوة; on that account its hāʾ in لم يتسنه is a pause marker, supported by forms such as سنوات, سانيت, and a poetic use of مسنتون.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r2.speaker: الفراء عن الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r2.claim: Al-Farra, quoted by al-Wahidi, allows سنة to derive from سننة; then لم يتسنه comes from لم يتسنن, with a final nūn dropped and a pause hāʾ added, like لم يتقضه.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r3.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r3.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi derives the word from مسنون, related to pouring; the drink remained undiminished, with the final nūn dropped and pause hāʾ supplied.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r4.claim: For readers retaining the hāʾ, سنة derives from سنهه, supported by the diminutive سنيهة and the verb سانهت; hāʾ is a root consonant, not a pause marker.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30#2/r5.claim: لم يتسنه means the food and drink did not change; literally, the years did not pass over it, as though time had not touched it, while Abu Ali's account also permits the sense that the drink did not dry up.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r1.claim: His estimate was based on what seemed true to him, so it is not culpable lying; the sleepers of the cave similarly said they had stayed a day or part of one.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r2.claim: Joseph's brothers likewise spoke from an apparent sign when they said Joseph's brother had stolen the cup and that they testified only to what they knew.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r3.claim: The stronger view is that the passer knew the interval resulted from death, since the purpose was to show resurrection and signs in himself or the donkey indicated death.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r4.claim: A reported etymology derives ʿām from ʿawm, swimming, because a year involves a long passage through which one cannot act freely.

RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r5.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم
RAZI-FULL:v7p30/r5.claim: These readers retain the hāʾ in connected recitation in لم يتسنه and the listed words اقتده، ماليه، سلطانيه، ماهيه; Hamza omits it throughout, while al-Kisa'i omits it in the first two and retains it in the others.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r1.claim: Unchanged food seems to support his short estimate, but this strengthens the lesson: the donkey's decayed bones then show God's power, since food usually spoils sooner than a donkey's remains.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r2.claim: Seeing perishable food preserved while bones had decayed and were then revived made the wonder more vivid and firmly established the proof in his mind.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r3.claim: Although لم يتسنه grammatically follows drink, food too can be described as unchanged, especially delicate food that spoils quickly; the reported food was figs and grapes, with grape juice and milk.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r4.claim: Ibn Masud's reading has وانظر إلى طعامك وهذا in the passage about inspecting the food.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r5.claim: The donkey's bones alone do not prove a hundred years, because God could make them decay instantly; their restoration to life is the miracle confirming the report of the duration.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r6.speaker: الضحاك
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak says the revival after death demonstrated the truth of resurrection.

RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r7.speaker: غيره
RAZI-FULL:v7p31/r7.claim: Another reported view says the sign was that the man returned young with black hair while his grandsons were old, with white beards and hair.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r1.claim: How means revive; God is said to نشر the dead, and 80:22 and 36:78–79 speak of reviving bones.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r2.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r2.claim: A reading ننشرها with nūn and shīn means spreading after folding: lifelessness is like being folded, and life restores active movement.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r3.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r3.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ننشزها with zāy, meaning to raise the bones, return each to its place, and join them together.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r4.speaker: النخعي
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r4.claim: Al-Nakha'i reads ننشزها with an active causative form; al-Akhfash explains it as raising, the same sense as the other readings.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r5.claim: All readings describe God arranging the bones in order, then spreading flesh, veins, nerves, and skin over them and raising each part beside the next.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r6.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted subject after فلما تبين له, namely that God can do all things; al-Razi calls this strained and says the phrase refers to witnessed revival.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r7.claim: After directly witnessing death and revival, the man says he knows God can do all things; the experience confirms and renews knowledge he already had by inference.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r8.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v7p32#2/r8.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read قال أعلم as an imperative; one explanation is that after the sign he commands himself to know this truth.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r1.claim: Making him a sign means honoring him and promising high religious and worldly rank, which is unsuitable for someone who died in unbelief and doubt.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r2.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r2.claim: Al-Farra explains the coordinating waw in ولنجعلك by an implied فعلنا ما فعلنا; otherwise looking at the donkey would be a condition for making him a sign.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r3.claim: The same implied-clause construction appears in 6:105 and 6:75: God made the signs or showed Abraham the kingdom for the stated purpose.
