RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r4.claim: Most commentators take the bones to be the donkey's bones; the lām in إلى العظام stands in place of a pronoun.

RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r5.speaker: قتادة والربيع وابن زيد
RAZI-FULL:v7p32/r5.claim: Qatada, al-Rabi, and Ibn Zayd identify the bones as the man's own, with his head and eyes revived while his remaining body reassembled; al-Razi rejects this as inconsistent with his estimate of one day and the whole-person wording.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the town with the place from which thousands fled fearing death; they were made to die, and a passerby who saw their exposed bones asked how God would revive them.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Ibn Zayd’s account as conflicting with the verse: it describes an uninhabited ruined town, and reviving it means rebuilding it and restoring residents.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه وقتادة والضحاك والربيع وعكرمة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.claim: Wahb, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ, and ʿIkrima say it was Jerusalem, devastated by the Babylonian Bukhtanaṣṣar; the account names Irmiyāʾ or ʿUzayr as the observer.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.speaker: السدي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the houses as collapsed roofs with walls fallen over them; al-Ṭabarī chooses this reading of the phrase “hollow upon their roofs.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.claim: Others interpret the phrase as a town empty of people while buildings remained; khāwiya can mean vacant or fallen, as in other Qurʾānic usages, and its root also denotes emptiness, hunger, or a belly emptied in childbirth.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r6.claim: The question “how” asks by what means the town could be revived; its apparent sense is rebuilding and repopulating a ruined city, expressing grief for the familiar place and its people, though it may also point to raising its dead.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r7.speaker: بعضهم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#2/r7.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits a view that the speaker doubted God’s ability to give life, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects interpreting the verse as doubt and says no doubt should be attributed here.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r1.claim: “One hundred years” is an accusative of time; ʿām means year and intensifies the sense, like a phrase such as “busy work.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r2.speaker: النقاش
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r2.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives ʿām from swimming: a year is called this because the sun swims through its orbit; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats this as equivalent to the root meaning “swim,” as in 21:33.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r3.claim: The apparent meaning of God causing death is that the soul was removed from the body.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r4.claim: A report says God appointed a Persian king to rebuild the town; another says after seventy years God sent the great Persian king Kushk, who completed its rebuilding in thirty years.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r5.claim: “Then He raised him” means God brought him back to life.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r6.claim: Reported possibilities for the voice asking how long he stayed include God, a heavenly voice, Gabriel, a prophet, or a surviving believer; the author prefers God, since the following words say God will raise the bones.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r7.speaker: أهل الكوفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r7.claim: The Kufans read “how long did you remain?” with assimilation of thāʾ into tāʾ because of their close articulation; al-Naḥḥās prefers clear pronunciation because the sounds have distinct articulation points.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r8.claim: The question particle kam is in the accusative as an adverb of time.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#3/r9.claim: The man reported his apparent perception rather than lying about an objectively longer interval.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r1.claim: The People of the Cave said they had stayed a day or part of a day despite their much longer actual stay; the account also compares the reply with the Prophet’s statement in the Dhū al-Yadayn incident.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r2.claim: Some say the statement was literally false but unpunished; in legal theory, falsehood is reporting contrary to fact regardless of knowledge, and prophets may unintentionally report inaccurately as they may forget.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r3.claim: The author prefers the first explanation: the speaker truthfully reported his perception rather than lying.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r4.speaker: ابن جريج وقتادة والربيع
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r4.claim: Ibn Jurayj, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ say he died in the morning and was revived before sunset; he thought one day had passed, then added “or part of a day” when he saw the remaining sun.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r5.claim: When told he had remained a hundred years, he saw the town’s rebuilt structures and trees, which showed him the elapsed time.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r6.claim: Ibn Masʿūd’s reading adds “and this is your food and drink” before saying it had not changed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r7.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r7.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif reads “look at your food and drink for a hundred years”; he also gives another form assimilating the command to look.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r8.speaker: الجمهور والأخوان
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#4/r8.claim: Most readers retain the hāʾ of “yatasannah” when connecting the recitation, while the two readers do not; all retain it when pausing.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r1.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r1.claim: Al-Naḥḥās says a reader who omits the hāʾ in connected speech may treat it as a pause marker; al-Mahdawī also gives analyses deriving the form from year-to-year dealings, with hāʾ either a root consonant or pause marker.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r2.speaker: مجاهِد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r2.claim: Mujāhid says the food and drink had not become putrid.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r3.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r3.claim: Al-Naḥḥās says the strongest derivation is from “year”: the passing years had not changed the food.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#5/r4.claim: Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī derives the word from a verb meaning water became altered, linking it to the “masnūn” clay of 15:26; al-Zajjāj rejects this because masnūn there means shaped or poured, not changed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r1.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih and others say God reassembled the donkey’s bones, clothed them with flesh, and then an angel breathed life into it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r2.speaker: الضحاك ووهب بن منبه
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Wahb instead say the donkey remained alive, tethered in its place, while only the man’s body died; people were prevented from seeing him and the donkey for the hundred years.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r3.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the waw in “and to make you a sign” as indicating a purpose attached to an implied action; alternatively it may be an inserted, redundant waw.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r4.speaker: الأعمش
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r4.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the sign was that the man returned at the age he had been at death while his children and grandchildren were old; ʿIkrima says he died at forty.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r5.speaker: علي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r5.claim: A report from ʿAlī says ʿUzayr left his pregnant wife at age fifty, returned after a hundred years still fifty, and found a son fifty years younger than him.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r6.claim: In Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, ʿUzayr’s prayer restores the sight of an elderly blind former servant, who recognizes him and alerts the Israelites; his son confirms him by a crescent-shaped birthmark between the shoulders.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r7.claim: Another account says everyone who knew the man had died, so he served as a sign to those then alive through the certain reports they had heard about him.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#6/r8.claim: The word may also refer to drought years: the food was unchanged by famine or by the passage of years and remained fresh.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r1.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the hundred-year death and revival itself is the greatest sign, and the man’s whole story remains a sign across time without restricting it to one feature.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r2.speaker: الكوفيون وابن عامر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r2.claim: The Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir read the verb with zāy, “raise them”; others read it with rāʾ, “revive them,” and a further reading has an active form of “spread/revive.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r3.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وأبو حيوة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ḥaywa use the “revive/spread” reading; it can be a synonym for raising the dead, while نشر also means unfolding a garment.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r4.speaker: مكي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r4.claim: Makkī prefers the zāy reading for the bones because it means raising one bone onto another in reconstruction; the bones do not live separately, while the man is what is revived.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r5.speaker: النخعي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r5.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī reads the verb with fatḥa on the first nūn and ḍamma on shīn and zāy; this reading is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r6.speaker: أبي بن كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r6.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reads the form with yāʾ, “we assemble/raise them.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#7/r7.claim: The verse likens flesh covering the bones to clothing; Labīd uses the same clothing image for Islam in his poetry.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r1.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r1.claim: Qatāda says God first created the man’s head and then showed him how the remaining bones were joined together as they were revived.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r2.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r2.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says that when the evidence became plain, the man acknowledged a power he had previously found difficult to conceive; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as imposing an unsupported and weak interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the phrase is not a confession of earlier denial; it is the exclamation of a believer reflecting on an extraordinary display of God’s power, which the author supports.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r4.speaker: أبو علي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r4.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains “I know” to mean that the man acquired a kind of knowledge through direct observation that he had not previously possessed; Qatāda and Makkī give this sense too.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r5.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r5.claim: Most readers pronounce “I know” with hamza qaṭʿ; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read it with hamza waṣl, which can be an angel’s command or the man addressing his own soul.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r6.speaker: مكي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r6.claim: Makkī says an order from God to know would be unlikely after the man had seen and acknowledged the proof, so self-address is a sound reading; the ʿAbd Allāh codex and Ibn ʿAbbās’s reading instead support a divine command to retain certain knowledge.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to read “it was said: know,” treating the command as God’s instruction after the man witnessed resurrection; he asks rhetorically whether this is better than Abraham’s instruction.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259#8/r8.claim: The author explains the verb as the man affirming that, through witnessing the resurrection, he now knows in a direct and certain way that God has power over everything.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r1.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r1.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ treat “or” as coordination by meaning: have you seen the one who disputed with Abraham, or the one who passed a ruined town?

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r10.speaker: القتبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r10.claim: Al-Qutbī is reported to identify the passerby as Isaiah in one of his positions; another report says he was Lot’s servant.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r11.speaker: وهب بن منبه وقتادة والربيع بن أنس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r11.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ identify the town as Jerusalem, which Bukhtanaṣṣar had destroyed; the food was said to be green figs and grapes and the drink wine, juice, or water.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r12.claim: In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās via Abū Ṣāliḥ, Bukhtanaṣṣar deported Israelites, including the learned ʿUzayr, to Babylon; ʿUzayr later stopped at a ruined town and wondered how God would revive it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r2.speaker: المبرد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad supplies an ellipsis: “Have you seen the one who disputed with Abraham—have you seen who he is?—like the one who passed a town.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r3.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حسين
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r3.claim: Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥusayn reads the waw in “or the one who passed” with fatḥa, treating it as coordination preceded by the interrogative alif of emphasis.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r4.claim: The word for town, qarya, is linked to people gathering there, as in the expression for collecting water.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r5.speaker: سليمان بن بريدة وناجية بن كعب وقتادة وابن عباس والربيع وعكرمة والضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r5.claim: Sulaymān ibn Burayda, Nājiya ibn Kaʿb, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk identify the passerby as ʿUzayr.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r6.speaker: وهب بن منبه وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير وعبد الله بن بكر بن مضر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r6.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih and others identify the passerby as the prophet Irmiyāʾ (Jeremiah).

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r7.speaker: ابن إسحاق
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r7.claim: Ibn Isḥāq identifies Irmiyāʾ as al-Khiḍr, a claim also attributed by al-Naqqāsh to Wahb; Ibn ʿAṭiyya questions it because al-Khiḍr was contemporary with Moses whereas this event was later.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r8.claim: The author says Irmiyāʾ could be al-Khiḍr if the sound view that al-Khiḍr remained alive from Moses onward is correct; if he died before the event, Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s objection stands.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r9.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:259/r9.claim: Mujāhid is reported to say the passerby was an unnamed man from the Children of Israel.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r1.claim: The bones may be those of the donkey or of the dead people whose revival astonished him.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r2.claim: Nanshizu means either revive the bones or raise and assemble them; kayfa is adverbial and the clause depicts the bones revived.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr, and Yaqub read nunshiruha, from God raising the dead; another reading derives it from nashara with the same sense.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r4.claim: The subject of 'when it became clear to him' is omitted and supplied by the following clause, or the preceding event explains what became clear.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259#2/r5.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'know' as an imperative, addressed either to the listener or reflexively to the speaker as a rebuke.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r1.claim: The construction is estimated as 'or have you seen the like of the one who passed'; the omitted phrase is understood from the preceding 'have you not seen.'

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r10.claim: The question 'How long did you remain?' is spoken by God; this is possible because the man believed after revival or was close to believing. Another view assigns it to an angel or prophet.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r11.claim: The man guessed 'a day or part of a day'; one account says he died at forenoon and awoke before sunset, first saying a day, then correcting himself after seeing the sun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r12.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r12.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r12.claim: Lam yatasannah means the food and drink had not changed; the word may derive from sanah with h as root or pause marker, or from a form related to al-hama al-masnun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r13.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r13.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r13.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read lam yatasan without final h in connected recitation; the dual food and drink take a singular pronoun because they form one kind.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r14.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r14.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r14.claim: The food may have been figs and grapes and the drink juice or milk, all preserved unchanged.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r15.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r15.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r15.claim: The donkey may be shown in scattered bones, or still safe where it was tied, preserved without water or fodder; the scattered bones better fit the scene and following verse.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r16.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r16.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r16.claim: The event made him a sign: he returned as a young man while his children were elderly, or read the Torah from memory and was recognized, after which people called him God's son.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r2.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r2.claim: The comparative particle is extra, yielding 'Have you not seen the one who disputed, or the one who passed?'

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r3.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r3.claim: The phrase is conjoined according to sense, as though it said, 'Have you not seen like the one who disputed, or like the one who passed?'

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r4.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r4.claim: Alternatively, these words are Abraham's reply to an opponent: if you claim to revive, revive as God revived the passerby.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r5.claim: The passerby is identified as Uzayr son of Sharahya, al-Khidr, or a disbeliever in resurrection; the last view is supported by the passage's sequence with Nimrod.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r6.claim: The village may be Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, the village from which thousands departed, or another place; qaryah derives from gathering.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r7.claim: The village is empty, its walls fallen onto its roofs; the speaker's question expresses either confessed inability and awe at revival or skeptical disbelief.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r8.claim: Anna is parsed as an adverb meaning 'when' or as a circumstantial expression meaning 'how.'

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:259/r9.claim: God either kept him dead for a hundred years or caused him to die and leave him dead for a hundred years before reviving him.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r1.claim: The opening 'or like the one' has an omitted 'Have you seen?' supplied by the earlier question; both expressions signal wonder, or the syntax follows meaning rather than wording.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r10.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r10.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r10.claim: لم يتسنه means it did not change; its final h may be radical or a pause h, deriving from سنة as سنهة or سنوة; Hamza and Kisāʾī omit h in connected reading but retain it at pause.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r11.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r11.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r11.claim: His donkey's bones had separated and decayed; alternatively, the donkey remained alive where tied for a hundred years without food or water, a great sign.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r12.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r12.claim: Ezra's return was a sign: one account says he arrived mounted and recited the Torah from memory after no one had recited it visibly before him; another says his children were old while he was young.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r13.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r13.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r13.claim: The bones are either the donkey's or the bones of the dead whose revival he questioned; nunsizuhā means move and raise them together, while Hijazi and Basran read nunshiruhā, 'revive them.'

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r14.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r14.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r14.claim: Clothing bones with flesh is a metaphor; in 'when it became clear to him' the understood complement is that God can do all things, or what had puzzled him: resurrection.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r15.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r15.speaker: حمزة وعلى
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r15.claim: They read aʿlam as an imperative: God tells Ezra to know, or Ezra addresses himself; the other reading is his statement that he knows.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r2.speaker: صاحب الكشف
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r2.claim: Al-Kashshāf's author says the kāf is redundant and alladhī coordinates with the person who disputed Abraham.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r3.speaker: الحسن
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r3.claim: Hasan identifies the passerby as an unbeliever in resurrection, linked with Nimrod by context and by the expression of incredulity.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r4.speaker: الأكثر
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r4.claim: Most identify the passerby as Ezra, who sought to witness revival and increase certainty, as Abraham had; his question admits ignorance of how and magnifies God's power.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r5.claim: The ruined town is Jerusalem, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar; it is also the town from which thousands had departed.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r6.claim: The roofs may have fallen together with their supports, or roofs fell first and walls then collapsed on them.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r7.claim: The question asks how God will revive the town's inhabitants after their death; God then caused the passerby to die for a hundred years and raised him.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r8.claim: His estimate of a day or part of one was conjecture; he died in the morning and awoke before sunset a century later, so he first saw a day then the remaining sun.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r9.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p126/r9.claim: His food was figs and grapes and his drink juice and milk; the fruit seemed freshly picked and the drink unchanged.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#2/r1.claim: Feeling a long interval as a day resembles resurrection passages: the unaware do not sense motion or time, and separation seems never to have occurred once reunion arrives.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r2.speaker: قيل
QASHANI:2:259#2/r2.claim: An earlier interpretation identifies the food as figs and grapes and the drink as wine and milk.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#2/r3.claim: Figs represent universal intelligibles with particulars latent in them, while grapes represent particulars retaining material adjuncts in cognition.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#2/r4.claim: Milk signifies useful knowledge such as revealed laws; wine signifies love, will, and knowledge of mystical realities.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#2/r5.claim: Unchanged food signifies knowledge deposited eternally in each soul according to its aptitude: material veils conceal but do not alter it, and a purified heart reveals it again.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r6.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:2:259#2/r6.claim: A prophetic report compares people to mines of gold and silver, supporting the idea that knowledge is latent in souls.

QASHANI:2:259#2/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#2/r7.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:2:259#2/r7.claim: A prophetic report calls wisdom the believer's lost property, supporting the recovery of veiled innate knowledge.

QASHANI:2:259#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#3/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#3/r1.claim: The donkey is the body: intact under the first two readings, but with decayed bones under the third.

QASHANI:2:259#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#3/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#3/r2.claim: God makes him a sign that resurrection is possible; the bones are raised, gathered, and clothed in flesh as the body is reconstructed.

QASHANI:2:259#3/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259#3/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259#3/r3.claim: When resurrection and reassembly become clear, he recognizes God's power over everything.

QASHANI:2:259/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r1.claim: The ruined town's passerby, commonly identified as ʿUzayr, is a seeker who wonders about revival before attaining certainty or readiness for the Reviver's manifestation.

QASHANI:2:259/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r2.claim: His death can signify remaining dead in ignorance, as in the cited verses; alternatively it may be voluntary death through spiritual discipline or natural death followed by a same-kind body's acquisition of perfection.

QASHANI:2:259/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r3.claim: The hundred years may count lunar cycles as eight years and four months, seasonal years as twenty-five years, or reflect the longevity of people then.

QASHANI:2:259/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r4.claim: After true life he estimates only a day because ignorance's long death is slight beside eternal life and, like a sleeper, he did not sense time; the interval could also be spiritual discipline or an unperceived period between deaths and return.

QASHANI:2:259/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r5.claim: One alternative is voluntary death during one of the proposed periods, understood as spiritual discipline and struggle in God's way.

QASHANI:2:259/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:259/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:259/r6.claim: Another alternative is natural death, with the soul attached after some interval to another body of its kind to acquire perfection without awareness of its former or later state.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r3.claim: “Khāwī” means empty; its related forms also refer to a collapsed house, hunger, a woman’s empty womb after childbirth, and food set aside for her.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r4.claim: “Arsh” is a roof or any structure made for shade, such as a vine trellis; the Qur’an also uses the root for what people build.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r5.claim: A report about building the mosque says the Prophet wanted a simple palm-frond shelter like Moses’ shelter.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p621#2/r6.claim: The cited rajaz line uses “khawā” for a camel’s posture, with its belly raised above the ground while resting or prostrating.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r1.claim: “Arsh” can also mean a building, as illustrated by a poem about razing a people’s structures.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r2.claim: “One hundred” is a known numerical rank, pluralized as hundreds; its weak final letter is omitted, its original form is mئة, and the verb means making or becoming one hundred.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r3.claim: A year is a known span; its alif derives from wāw, as shown by “years.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r4.speaker: النقاش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r4.claim: Al-Naqqash proposes that “year” is a verbal noun like swimming, named because the sun swims through its orbit; the cited Qur’anic phrase supports the swimming image.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r6.claim: If the hāʾ of “yatassannah” is original, the word derives from year; diminutive, plural, and Hijazi verb forms support that analysis.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r7.speaker: المبرد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r7.claim: Al-Mubarrad treats the final hāʾ as a pause marker; then the weak final letter is omitted under jussive mood and the word derives from year, with further proposed derivations from change or from altered “molded.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r8.speaker: أبو عمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r8.claim: Abu Umar derives the form from “masnūn” meaning changed, with sound changes avoiding repeated consonants; al-Zajjaj rejects this because “masnūn” means shaped on a path.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r9.speaker: النقاش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p622/r9.claim: Al-Naqqash derives “yatassannah” from water that has not become stale; grammarians object that the expected form would be “yata’assan.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r2.claim: The majority read “aw” with a still wāw and explain it as either differentiation or a choice that heightens wonder at the two examples.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r3.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حسين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r3.claim: Abu Sufyan ibn Husayn reads the wāw open, with an interrogative hamza understood: “Did you see the like of the one who passed?”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r4.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r4.claim: Most exegetes coordinate the second example by meaning with the first, since “Have you not seen?” means “Have you seen?”; Arabic permits such coordination by sense, though it is not analogically productive.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted “did you see the like of” from the preceding expression of wonder; Abu Hayyan prefers this straightforward ellipsis to coordination by sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r6.claim: Some call the kāf redundant so that “the one” coordinates directly with the earlier “one”; another analysis treats kāf as a noun governed by the preposition, a recognized but remote use.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p630/r7.claim: Abu Hayyan finds the nominal kāf analysis linguistically possible but remote; he judges the omitted-verb explanation preferable and notes that coordination by sense is not analogical.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r1.speaker: علي وابن عباس وعكرمة وأبو العالية وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة والربيع والضحاك والسدي ومقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r1.claim: These authorities identify the passerby as Uzayr.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r2.speaker: وهب ومجاهد وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير وبكر بن مضر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r2.claim: These authorities identify the passerby as Jeremiah; Ibn Ishaq calls him Jeremiah who is al-Khidr, as transmitted from Wahb by al-Naqqash.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects identifying the passerby with al-Khidr because Khidr was Moses’ contemporary whereas this man lived later, though one of his teachers allows Khidr as a long-lived survivor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r4.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r4.claim: Al-Hasan says the passerby was an unnamed unbeliever riding a donkey and carrying a basket of figs; other reports name an Israelite, Lot’s servant, or Shuʿyaʾ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r5.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r5.claim: Al-Suhayli, citing al-Qutaybi, says the one who revived the city was the Persian Lusak.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r6.speaker: وهب وقتادة والضحاك وعكرمة والربيع
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r6.claim: These authorities identify the city as Jerusalem; other locations proposed are a nearby grape village, the Holy Land, al-Muʾtafikah, the village from which people fled death, Heraclius’ monastery, Shabur Abad, and Salmayadh.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r7.speaker: السدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r7.claim: Al-Suddi says the village was empty of inhabitants but standing; another report says its walls had collapsed over its roofs, and على may mean “with” its buildings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p631/r8.claim: The circumstantial clause may modify the passerby or the village; treating it as a delayed adjective of the indefinite village is less likely because of the wāw. The preposition attaches to an implied “settled” if empty, or to “collapsed” if ruinous.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r1.claim: The speaker asking how long the man had stayed is apparently God, given the later “how We raise”; alternatives are a heavenly caller, Gabriel, a prophet, or a believer who witnessed the death and lived until the revival. The text does not say God spoke face-to-face.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reasons that the revived man was no longer an unbeliever, so God could address him; Abu Hayyan notes no text says the speech was direct.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r3.claim: “How long?” is a temporal adverbial question asking the duration of his being dead, as a question that elicits acknowledgment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r4.speaker: ابن جريج وقتادة والربيع
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r4.claim: They say he died in the morning and revived before sunset a century later, first guessing “a day” before noticing the remaining sun and revising to “part of a day.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633#2/r5.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers reading أو as correction rather than uncertainty: once the sun appeared, the man withdrew his mistaken guess and confidently said it was part of a day; “part” can denote most of something.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r1.claim: One historical account says Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem after Israel’s wrongdoing, and Jeremiah or Uzayr stood by the great mound created from the city’s soil.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari regards the passerby as an unbeliever in resurrection, suggested by the sequence after Nimrod and the question “how”; another view says Uzayr or Khidr sought firsthand reassurance like Abraham.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r3.speaker: أبو علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r3.claim: Abu Ali argues the passerby cannot be a prophet because prophets do not doubt in this way.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r4.claim: Life and death may be metaphorical for a city’s rebuilding and ruin, or literal for its inhabitants; the literal reading requires an implied “people” or a reference to their decayed remains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r5.claim: On the metaphorical reading, the question laments the ruined city of his loved ones and prompts reflection; on the literal reading it recognizes the inability to know how resurrection works while magnifying God, not doubting His power.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r6.speaker: الطبري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r6.claim: Al-Tabari cites an interpretation that the question was doubt in God’s power, which explains why the man received a personal demonstration.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r7.claim: God caused the man to live again, with movement and the ability to travel.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p633/r8.claim: A report says after seventy years God protected the dead man from animals and sight, directed Persian king Lusak to rebuild Jerusalem with thousands of foremen and workers, destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito, and returned Israelites who rebuilt the city over thirty years.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r1.claim: Abu Hayyan says adding wāw to a clause negated by لم is no better than omitting it; both are eloquent and occur in the Qur’an, so the claim that لم is very rare is mistaken.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r2.claim: One account says God revived the man’s eyes first while his body remained dead, then restored him as he watched scattered donkey bones gather and receive flesh; another says the donkey brayed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r3.claim: Another account says he watched Jerusalem rebuild while the donkey remained exactly as tied, and the mountain endured a century of wind, rain, sun, and cold; Wahb and al-Dahhak say the donkey remained standing untouched.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the donkey’s survival for a century without food or water one of the greatest signs, like preserving the food and drink.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r5.claim: “To make you a sign” may have an extra wāw, attach to an implied “we showed you,” or attach to an implied later “we did this”; each links the sign to the revival and preservation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r6.speaker: الأعمش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r6.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the sign was that the man returned at the same youthful age at which he died while his descendants had become old; Ikrima specifies that he was forty and his sons over a hundred.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635#2/r7.claim: Other explanations make him a sign because everyone who knew him had died, or because he returned claiming to be Uzayr and recited the Torah from memory without error, prompting people to call him God’s son.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r1.claim: A story about Uzayr says he escaped Babylon, reached Heraclius’ monastery by the Tigris, ate fruit and pressed grapes among the empty orchards, then wondered at the ruined village without doubting resurrection; another says his drink was milk.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r2.claim: Another account says the figs, grapes, and drink remained fresh and unchanged as he left them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r3.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi omit the hāʾ in connected recitation as a pause marker; the other seven retain it in connection and pause. The hāʾ is apparently original, though pause-like pronunciation remains possible.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r4.speaker: أبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r4.claim: Ubayy reads “lam yasnah” with assimilation of tāʾ into sīn, as in a similar assimilation elsewhere.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r5.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وغيره
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r5.claim: Talha ibn Musarrif and others read “for one hundred years” instead of “it did not change.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r6.speaker: عبد الله
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r6.claim: Abdullah reads “and this is your drink; it did not change.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r7.claim: The singular pronoun in “yatassannah” may refer only to the drink, with a parallel clause about food omitted, or to food and drink jointly treated as one because they are paired or mean sustenance; the negated clause is circumstantial.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p635/r8.claim: Some grammarians prefer coordinating a clause negated by لم with wāw, while others say لما is preferable; poetic lines illustrate the construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r1.claim: Abu Hayyan says the Torah had never been recited aloud before Uzayr and that his entire death and return is an enduring sign for people of every age, so no single detail needs to be privileged.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r2.claim: “The people” may mean his surviving contemporaries or all people through the end of time.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r3.speaker: قتادة والضحاك والربيع وابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r3.claim: These authorities say the bones are his; other views take them as the donkey’s or both. Al-Zamakhshari adds the dead people of the village, which Abu Hayyan rejects because they were not revived there.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r4.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers the donkey’s bones: the command follows the man’s resurrection and dialogue, and “its bones” can be understood by an omitted possessive or by the definite article replacing a pronoun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r5.speaker: الحرميان وأبو عمرو
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r5.claim: The two Meccan readers and Abu Amr read “nunshiruhā” with ḍamma on nūn and kasra-like rāʾ; Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, and Aban read it with fatḥa. Both derive from forms meaning revive, though نشر may also evoke unfolding bones after death.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r6.speaker: باقي السبعة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p636/r6.claim: The remaining canonical readers use zāy in “nunshizuhā,” meaning move or raise the bones together for reconstruction; other reported vocalizations vary the initial or medial vowels.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r1.speaker: أبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r1.claim: Ubayy reads “how we create them,” using the verb for creation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r2.claim: Some argue that bones cannot be alive individually and prefer the zāy reading as joining them; they understand God as raising them from the earth into the body. Abu Hayyan rejects its superiority because the rāʾ reading is mutawātir.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r3.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects parsing “how we raise them” as a circumstantial clause describing living bones: a full interrogative clause cannot be a circumstantial adjunct, though كيف alone can be.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r4.claim: He parses the interrogative clause as an object of the visual verb when it is syntactically suspended by a question, and as a substitute for “the state of the bones”: see their state, how God raises them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p637/r5.claim: Suspended interrogatives privilege grammatical form over intended question meaning; Arabic also has constructions where meaning overrides form, and he develops this issue in his grammatical work after a question from Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId about a hadith.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r1.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the claim that “to make you a sign” is syntactically advanced in wording but delayed in rank; the looks are coordinated in their stated order.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r2.claim: This episode is exceptionally strong evidence for resurrection because death and revival were witnessed in this world.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r3.claim: Most readers use the active “tabayyana”; Ibn Abbas reads it passive, and Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads a passive form without tāʾ. The active verb’s implied subject is the manner of revival that had seemed strange.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r4.speaker: الطبري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r4.claim: Al-Tabari says the man saw clearly what he had previously thought beyond God’s power; Ibn Atiyya rejects this for imposing the weak interpretation that he doubted resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted “that God can do everything” as the subject of “became clear,” repeated in the man’s next statement; Abu Hayyan says this is not grammatical “competition” because the two governing verbs do not share a coordinated construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639#2/r6.claim: The second clause is governed by “he said,” not “became clear”; the standard cases of shared government involve a conjunction or another genuine relation between the governing expressions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r1.claim: “Clothing” is literally what covers the body and here metaphorically names flesh covering bone; the image is especially apt as a concrete thing covering another concrete thing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r2.claim: A report says the man watched flesh, nerves, and veins rejoin; the apparent wording indicates God addressed him after he was fully revived, not while only part of him lived.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r3.claim: The sequence of commands to look suggests the bones are not the man’s own, unless the verbs for raising and covering stand for having raised and covered them already.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r4.claim: Each command to inspect the food, drink, and donkey is separated because each is a distinct, powerful miracle; unchanged food and drink are first because perishable things enduring a century are more striking than a living donkey that can forage.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r5.claim: The Prophet describes a stray camel as able to drink and eat trees until its owner arrives, illustrating why a living animal could survive naturally.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p639/r6.claim: The third look is not an independent sign: it explains what to inspect about the donkey, namely its bones rising and being assembled and clothed with flesh.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r1.claim: One grammatical option makes the passerby address himself as a separate addressee, as in Arabic self-address expressions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r2.speaker: الجعبي عن أبي بكر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641#2/r2.claim: A report from Abū Bakr reads أعلم as a command in form IV; the agent of قال is apparently God, ordering the passerby to tell others what he witnessed, though another parsing allows the passerby as agent.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r1.claim: The adverbial-genitive construction lacks a cited parallel in this grammatical pattern; Arabic usage also avoids juxtaposing two such clauses without a connector.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r2.claim: Zamakhshari analyzes the agent of تبين as omitted and supplied by the later clause; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because deletion conflicts with the proposed subject ellipsis and the Basran account.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r3.claim: On Ibn ʿAbbās’s reading, the prepositional phrase functions as the passive-subject substitute.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r4.speaker: ابن السميفع
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r4.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfa’s reading has an implicit subject: God made the matter clear to the passerby.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r5.claim: The majority read قال actively and أعلم as a first-person imperfect uttered by the passerby as reflective recognition, like a person amazed by something strange.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r6.speaker: أبو علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r6.claim: Abū ʿAlī glosses أعلم as acquiring direct, witnessed knowledge of what the passerby previously knew only unseen.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r7.speaker: أبو رجاء، وحمزة، والكسائي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r7.claim: Their command reading اعلم addresses the passerby, with God or an angel speaking for God as the implied agent.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r8.speaker: عبد الله والأعمش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p641/r8.claim: Their reading قيل اعلم uses a passive verb whose implicit passive subject is the command itself, not a following clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649/r1.claim: The three stories use eloquent question-and-answer dialogue with repeated قال and little coordination: when meaning itself connects successive clauses, an added conjunction is better omitted.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r1.claim: Laḥman is the second object of naksūhā, as with a verb of giving; clothing the bones in flesh is metaphorical, like Labīd's verse about wearing Islam as a cloak.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r2.claim: For falammā tabayyana, one view supplies an implicit subject such as the manner in which revival became clear; the author prefers it over al-Zamakhsharī's 'what had confused him' because the context supports the former.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī analyzes tabayyana and aʿlama by syntactic attraction: anna Allāha can be the subject of the first and object of the second, with the second verb governing and the first subject omitted.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says this is the preferred Basran form of tanāzuʿ, illustrated by Q 18:96 and 69:19; he says first-verb governance would require a different object pronoun construction.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#10/r5.claim: The Shaykh objects that tanāzuʿ requires the two governors to share a syntactic link; here the second verb is governed by qāla (the answer to lammā), while tabayyana is governed within the lammā clause, so the verbs do not compete for one constituent.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r1.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r1.claim: The Shaykh notes that grammarians do not analyze unlinked sequences such as 'when he came, I struck Zayd' as tanāzuʿ, and rejects al-Zamakhsharī's alleged competition between tabayyana and aʿlama.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r2.claim: The Shaykh also sees inconsistency in calling tabayyana's subject 'omitted' after calling it 'implicit'; if deletion is intended, that is al-Kisāʾī's account, since he disallows a hidden subject before its later expression.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r3.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r3.claim: The Shaykh cites poetry to debate whether an unexpressed subject can be anticipated before its later mention, adducing taʿfaqu bi-l-arṭā and the line huwīnani wa-hawaytu.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#11/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads tabayyana passively, with the following prepositional phrase as deputy subject; Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads ybayyanu without tāʾ, also passive, with an understood 'manner of revival' or the prepositional phrase as deputy subject.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r1.claim: The majority read qāla actively. With Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī's imperative aʿlam ('know'), the speaker may be God or an angel addressing the passer, or the passer may address himself by treating himself as another person (tajrīd).

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the passer's self-address tajrīd, as if he detached a speaker from himself; several cited poems use such self-address.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r3.claim: On the other readers' present-tense aʿlam, the passer is the subject and says, 'I know.'

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r4.speaker: الأعمش
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r4.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads qīla passively; its deputy subject may be the verbal noun or the following clause, as in an earlier discussion in the sūrah.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#12/r5.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī have the imperative aʿlam; most others have first-person aʿlam, while al-Jaʿfī from Abū Bakr has the imperative of aʿlama. The anna clause fills both objects, or one with the other omitted, under the prior disagreement.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r1.claim: The clause wa-hiya khāwiyah has five proposed functions: circumstantial of the passer; circumstantial of the town (if 'on its roofs' modifies it or a bare indefinite can take a circumstantial); circumstantial of its roofs, fronted; or of the possessive pronoun in 'its roofs'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows the circumstantial to come from the pronoun attached to ʿurūsh, with the relation of possession as governor; the author calls this weak but eased by the roofs being part of the town.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r3.claim: A fifth option makes wa-hiya khāwiyah an adjective of qaryah, although the author notes the usual objection that wāw does not separate adjective and noun; al-Zamakhsharī explains it as emphasizing attachment, following Ibn Jinnī.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#2/r4.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ's detailed dependencies tie the descriptive/circumstantial options to whether ʿalā ʿurūshihā is a repeated-preposition substitute for qaryah or an adjective; the author says this argument has an evident problem.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r1.claim: ʿAlā ʿurūshihā can be a badal of qaryah with the preposition repeated, an adjective ('a town fallen upon its roofs'), a complement of khāwiyah meaning collapsed, or attached to an omitted thābit ('standing') if khāwiyah means empty of inhabitants; the author says the last is unsupported.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r2.claim: Some take ʿalā to mean maʿa ('with'), and ʿurūsh then means the buildings themselves.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r3.claim: Khāwī means empty or vacant and has several related forms; khawāʾ may describe an empty house, hunger from an empty belly, level terrain, or a camel lifting its side from the ground.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r4.claim: A poetic line uses khawāʾ for a camel holding its side above the ground.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#3/r5.claim: ʿUrūsh is the plural of ʿarsh, a house roof or anything built for shade; another view uses it for the building itself, supported by a line about toppling a people's structures.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r1.claim: In annā yuhyī, annā can mean 'when' (then temporal) or 'how' (then circumstantial); the apparent sense is 'how', governed by yuhyī, as is baʿda.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ assigns annā a circumstantial position when it means 'how'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r3.claim: The revival and death may be figurative for rebuilding and ruin, or literal with 'the inhabitants' supplied; hadhihi may instead point to the decayed bones and scattered bodies of the townspeople.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r4.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ says miʾata ʿāmin is a time adverb by sense ('kept him for a hundred years'), or supplies an omitted fa-labitha; the author says both repairs are unnecessary because God made him dead for that duration.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r5.claim: Miʾah is a known unit of one hundred with deleted final yāʾ, inferred from amʾaytu ('made into a hundred'); its plural is miʾāt, with the poetic form miʾūn rare.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r6.speaker: النقاش
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r6.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives ʿām from ʿāmah/ʿāwmah, a year-long solar circuit, linking it to swimming and Q 36:40; on this account ʿām and ʿawm parallel qawl and qāl.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#4/r7.claim: The wāw in ʿām is shown by the diminutive ʿuwaym and plural aʿwām.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r1.claim: Kam is an accusative time adverb governed by labithta, with an omitted specification such as 'days' or 'time'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r2.claim: Aw in yawman aw baʿḍa yawm most likely means bal ('rather'), not doubt; bal labithta coordinates with an omitted 'I did not stay a day or part of one'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r3.claim: Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Kathīr pronounce the thāʾ distinctly throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers assimilate it.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r4.claim: Lam yat as a circumstantial clause is debated: some prefer wāw before imperfect negation with lam, others prefer mā or lammā; both rules are false because Qurʾān has examples with and without wāw, including Q 3:174 and 6:93.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r5.claim: The singular pronoun in lam yatasannah after food and drink is explained because they form one nourishment, or because it refers to the nearer drink and the food clause is elided (or its nonchange follows a fortiori); a third account uses singular for dual, which the author rejects.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r6.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī retain hāʾ at pause but drop it in connected speech; the other readers retain it in both positions. For their reading it marks pause, while the common reading may retain a pause marker in connection or have original hāʾ.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#5/r7.claim: If yatasannah derives from sanah (year), its deleted root lām is wāw, as shown by the diminutive and plural sanīyah/sanawāt and forms such as sānaytu and asnata al-qawm.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r1.claim: Abū ʿAmr derives yatasannah from masnūn ('changed'), with three adjacent nūns simplified through substitution and sound change; al-Zajjāj rejects this because masnūn means molded or poured along a way.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r2.speaker: النقاش
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r2.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives the form from asina al-māʾ ('water changed'); grammarians reject the derivation as morphologically faulty, though the sense is right, and the author offers a possible metathesis explanation.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r3.claim: The hāʾ may instead be a root consonant in the Hijazi form of sanah; diminutive, plural, verb, and a poetic line support sanīhah, sanīhāt, and sānahat.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r4.claim: Lam yatasannah means that the food and drink did not change through the years; this is better than Abū al-Baqāʾ's 'no years passed over it', which contradicts the stated hundred years.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r5.speaker: أبي
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#6/r5.claim: Ubayy reads lam yasnah, assimilating the tāʾ into the sīn, like the assimilation in Q 37:8; Ṭalḥah b. Muṣarrif reads lamʾiata sanah.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r1.claim: Wa-li-najʿalaka may attach to an omitted verb ('We did this to make you a sign'), coordinate with an omitted purpose, or—with an extra wāw—attach to 'look at your donkey'; the author rejects claims of fronting and back-shifting among the three commands to look.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#7/r2.claim: The lām is purposive and the following verb is subjunctive with an implicit an; āyah is the second object of jaʿala in its 'make/transform' sense, and li-l-nās modifies āyah, with al either referring to the surviving townsfolk or humanity in general.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r1.claim: Kayfa is an accusative circumstantial expression governed by nanshizuhā, with the object pronoun as its referent; unẓur cannot govern an interrogative because it has clause-initial position.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ takes both kayfa and the interrogative clause as a circumstantial phrase for the bones; the author rejects this because an interrogative clause cannot itself be a circumstantial, though kayfa alone can.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r3.claim: The author instead parses the whole 'how We raise them' clause as a substitute for al-ʿiẓām, governed by the suspended visual verb; an omitted 'state of' makes the substitution grammatical, as in 'I knew Zayd: whose father is he?'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#8/r4.claim: Abū ʿAmr and the Ḥijāzī readers pronounce nunshiruha with rāʾ; the remaining readers have nunshizuha with zāy, while Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Nakhaʿī transmit additional vowel and consonant variants.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r1.claim: The Ḥijāzī rāʾ reading derives from anshara Allāh al-mawtā ('God revived the dead'); Ibn ʿAbbās's triliteral nashara can mean the same, or spreading/unfolding as a metaphor for revival, though its usual intransitive reflexive sense cannot fit this transitive construction.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r2.claim: A poem uses nāshir for a dead person who has come back to life, showing intransitive nashara meaning 'to live again'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r3.claim: The zāy reading comes from nashz ('elevation'): the bones are moved and raised into alignment for revival.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah objects that nushūz is gradual rising and does not naturally mean lifting bones together; he supports this sense with expressions for a camel's tooth rising and 'rise, and they rose'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r5.claim: With ḍamma, nunshiz is from anshaza; with fatḥa it is from nashaza, both used transitively. A yāʾ reading makes God the subject, and Ubayy reads nunshiʾuhā from nashʾah.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259#9/r6.claim: Some prefer zāy because bones revive by joining together, not individually; the author rejects the claim that bones cannot be alive, citing Q 36:78, and supplies the omitted reference 'the donkey's bones'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r1.claim: Most read aw with a quiescent wāw as a division between examples; another view makes it a choice between wonders. Abū Sufyān b. Ḥusayn reads a fatḥa, parsing a conjunction wāw preceded by an interrogative hamza.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r2.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r2.claim: One parse coordinates ka-alladhī by sense with alam tara, yielding 'Have you seen the one who disputed Abraham, or the one who passed a town?'; such semantic coordination is attested in poetry but grammarians say it is not analogically productive.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r3.claim: A second, strong parse supplies an omitted raʾayta, cued by alam tara; both clauses then express wonder, and the author favors this over semantic coordination because ellipsis is common.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r4.claim: A third analysis treats the kāf as extra, as in Q 42:11 and a poetic example; it is weak because words should not be assumed extra without need.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r5.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r5.claim: Al-Akhfash treats kāf as a noun meaning 'like'; the author calls this correct by the evidence, construing the phrase as 'or the like of the one who passed', though most Basrans disagree.

SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:259/r6.claim: Evidence for nominal kāf includes its parallel use with mithl as a subject in poetry and its ability to take prepositions and serve as their complement.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب، ابن عباس، الحسن، قتادة، السدي، سليمان بن بريدة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r1.claim: The well-known view identifies the passerby as ʿUzayr; ʿAlī is reported to say this, and Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and Sulaymān ibn Burayda also held it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه، عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r2.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr identify the passerby as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r3.claim: In a report transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq from Wahb, the figure is called al-Khiḍr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r4.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r4.claim: An unnamed Syrian informant identifies him as Ḥizqīl ibn Būrā.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r5.speaker: مجاهد بن جبر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r5.claim: Mujāhid identifies him simply as a man from the Children of Israel.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p687/r6.claim: The village is famously identified as Jerusalem, after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it and killed its inhabitants; khāwiyah means empty of people, from an Arabic expression for a vacant house.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r1.claim: The village's roofs and walls had fallen into its open spaces; the man reflected on how it could return to life after such ruin.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r2.claim: The town was rebuilt seventy years after the man's death, its population grew, and the Israelites returned before God revived him after a century.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r3.claim: God first revived the man's eyes so he could watch how his body would be restored; revived near the end of the day, he thought only a day or part had passed because the sun remained.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r4.claim: His grapes, figs, and juice remained unchanged for a hundred years, while the donkey's revival was shown before his eyes as a sign for people and evidence of resurrection.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r5.claim: The word nanshizuhā, with zāy, means raising the bones and fitting them together one over another.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r6.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r6.claim: A report says the Prophet recited the word with zāy; al-Ḥākim called its chain sound, though the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections did not include it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r7.claim: Mujāhid explains the variant recitation nanshuruhā, with rāʾ, as “revive them.”

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r8.speaker: السدي وغيره
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r8.claim: Al-Suddī and others say the donkey's scattered bones were gathered by a wind and reassembled; flesh, sinew, veins, and skin were restored, and an angel breathed into its nostrils until it brayed before ʿUzayr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r9.speaker: قراءة أخرى
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p688/r9.claim: Another recitation makes the final verb a command, “Know,” addressed to the man rather than his statement, “I know.”

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r1.speaker: author
