BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r1.claim: Resurrection is a uniquely divine sign. The sequence answers a claimant to divine power, shows resurrection to an astonished skeptic, then addresses a faithful seeker of certainty, each phrased for that person's state.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r10.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r10.claim: One hundred is singled out as complete in the units-and-tens count; what is completed by the third stage makes further repetition unnecessary.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r2.claim: The opening can be read as asking whether the Prophet saw the earlier disputant or whether his people resemble the passerby; the stories of earlier peoples serve as admonitions.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r3.claim: Al-Raḍī's grammatical observation is that interrogative هل can function with a negative force, allowing an إلا construction that turns the question into an affirmative assertion.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r4.claim: Passing by means proceeding along a route while turning one's attention to something encountered on the way.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r5.claim: The ruined town is identified either as the town from which thousands had once departed or as Jerusalem; it lay collapsed over its roofs, or empty while its roofs remained.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r6.claim: Khāwiya describes something emptied of what would sustain it physically or spiritually; the makeshift structures called roofs suggest the world's frailty beside a fortified dwelling.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r7.claim: The passerby asks how God could restore the ruined town to a populated, thriving state after its death.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r8.claim: The word annā spans how, where, and when; the question expresses doubt about resurrection's manner, place, and time, arising from the soul's demand to understand what lies beyond its reach.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p505/r9.claim: The skeptic's certainty about how resurrection works was deferred through a century of death so his soul could be prepared for knowledge; the long interval let the donkey decay while the food and drink remained unchanged.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r1.claim: The author says the event was done so the man could become certain of divine power; after he is raised, the account turns to his experience and its extraordinary signs.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r10.claim: The reading أعلم as a first-person verb conveys his own knowledge, while an imperative reading teaches the lesson to others; together they encompass learning and teaching.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r11.claim: The present tense in أعلم may indicate that he has always known God's power; his earlier astonishment then concerned how that power works, not whether God can do it.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r12.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r12.claim: God's power is witnessed through the wise causes that sight can discern, extending recognition of divine agency from resurrection to every act and detail.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r13.claim: The story corrects the disputant's sophistry: the life relevant to divine sovereignty is real resurrection after death, not merely sparing someone who otherwise deserved execution.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r14.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r14.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r14.claim: The surah gradually establishes resurrection through recurring references to afterlife and revival, preparing deniers for Abraham's account as proof from the Qur'an, whose inimitable testimony is God's own testimony.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r2.claim: The questioner who asks how long the man slept may be God or someone whose speech originates with God; seeing the preserved food made the man guess a day, then part of a day, before inspecting the donkey.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r3.claim: A hundred years expresses spaciousness, duration, and length; the preserved figs and juice, among the quickest foods to spoil, demonstrate protection across that span.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r4.claim: The reading with a silent hāʾ of pause in لم يتسنه presents the report of no change as certain and wholly beyond doubt.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r5.claim: The preserved perishable food and the donkey reduced to bones contrast a moist thing kept intact with a dry thing dismantled, displaying God's power over both.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r6.claim: The man's whole story is a sign to all people, a worldly instance that anticipates the Hour, resurrection, and gathering in the next life.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r7.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r7.claim: The reading with rāʾ derives from nashr, restoring what perished to its former form; the reading with zāy derives from nashz, raising and making something appear.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r8.claim: Reassembling the donkey's bones and clothing them with flesh makes the resurrection visible as an argument against deniers and skeptics.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r9.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p506/r9.claim: The form تبيّن suggests that the man hesitated between examining the two signs until the matter shown to him settled and his prior estimate disappeared.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p508/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p508/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p508/r2.claim: The three accounts form stages: the denier ends in humiliation, the skeptic who doubted learns and believes, and the believer advances to certainty and vision of God's dominion in the earthly realm.

DURR-FULL:v2p25/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r4.claim: ʿAlī identifies the passerby as the prophet Ezra, who left his city young, saw it ruined, wondered how God would revive it, then died for a century; his eyes were recreated first as he watched the bones reassemble and receive flesh.

DURR-FULL:v2p25/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r5.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām identifies the man who died for a hundred years and was revived as Ezra.

DURR-FULL:v2p25/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p25/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies Ezra ibn Sarukha as the person in the verse.

DURR-FULL:v2p27/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p27/r1.speaker: عكرمة وقتادة وسليمان بن بريدة والضحاك والسدي
DURR-FULL:v2p27/r1.claim: Ikrimah, Qatādah, Sulaymān ibn Buraydah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī give the same identification as the preceding report: the passerby is Ezra.

DURR-FULL:v2p27/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p27/r2.speaker: ابن عباس وكعب والحسن ووهب
DURR-FULL:v2p27/r2.claim: A composite report says Ezra asked in wonder, not doubt, how the ruined place could live again; after a century he watched his body and donkey reconstructed, while his food and drink remained unchanged, as proof of resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r1.claim: Ezra recovered a decayed Torah his father had hidden; two stars entered his body and enabled him to renew it. The Jews called him God’s son because of this event; Ibn Abbas calls the episode a sign for Israel.

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r2.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr identifies the passerby as the prophet Urmiyā (Jeremiah).

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r3.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah asked how God would revive Jerusalem after its destruction, then died for a century and watched its bones rejoin and receive flesh; his food was figs and water.

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r4.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r4.claim: Ikrimah identifies the ruined village as Jerusalem, which Nebuchadnezzar destroyed; Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Rabīʿ agree.

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r5.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r5.claim: A Syrian man identified the revived man as Ḥizqīl ibn Būzā.

DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p28#2/r6.claim: Al-Hasan places the events of Ezra and Nebuchadnezzar in an interval between prophetic eras.

DURR-FULL:v2p28/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v2p28/r1.claim: The report describes the donkey’s bones reassembled, then clothed with flesh and skin and revived; Ezra saw this as proof that God can revive the dead and all things.

DURR-FULL:v2p28/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p28/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p28/r2.claim: The narrative says a woman who had been Ezra’s servant recognized him after he restored her sight and mobility; his son and descendants verified his identity, and the Israelites asked him to restore the Torah.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r1.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r1.claim: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ dates Ezra’s story between Jesus and Muhammad.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r10.claim: In a discussion with Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, Ibn Abbas says the phrase means the years did not change the food and cites Arabic poetry using the root for becoming stale.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r2.claim: Wahb instead places Ezra and Nebuchadnezzar’s story between Jesus and Solomon.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses khāwiyah as ruined; Qatādah says it means uninhabited.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r4.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r4.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk glosses the structures’ ʿurūsh as their roofs; al-Suddī says they had collapsed onto their roofs.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r5.claim: Qatādah paraphrases the question as asking how God could rebuild the village after its ruin.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r6.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r6.claim: Al-Hasan says the man died at midmorning and was revived near sunset; his eyes were created first so he could watch a bone return to its place.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r7.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r7.claim: Qatādah says the man thought he had been there a day or part of one because he still saw some sunlight.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r8.claim: Qatādah identifies the food as a basket of figs and the drink as a jar of pressed juice; Mujahid instead calls the drink a jar of wine.

DURR-FULL:v2p29/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p29/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas explains lam yatasannah as remaining unchanged; Mujahid glosses it as not becoming rotten.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r1.claim: In the codex review under ʿUthmān, a reading written as lam yatasannan was corrected to lam yatasannah; the passage also records corrections to other verses.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r10.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r10.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the phrase as bringing the bones to life.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas reads the phrase as qāla aʿlam, understanding the words as a statement said to the man; another report says he read it that way because the man was no greater than Abraham, to whom God said to know.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r2.speaker: عثمان
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r2.claim: When Zayd asked about the spelling lam yatasannan or lam yatasannah, ʿUthmān instructed them to put a final hāʾ in the word.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r3.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r3.claim: Ikrimah says Ezra was revived as a young man aged 140 while his sons were a century old and grey-haired; Ibn Masʿūd is also said to give this account.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses nunshizuhā as raising or reassembling the bones.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the food and drink had not spoiled over a hundred years, and explains the bones as raised member by member.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r6.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r6.claim: Zayd ibn Thābit reports that the Prophet read nunshizuhā with zāy.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r7.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r7.claim: Zayd’s personal reading also used zāy, which he marked distinctly in his codex; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb likewise read it with zāy.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas read the word with rāʾ, nunshuruhā; ʿAṭāʾ and al-Hasan are also reported to read it with rāʾ.

DURR-FULL:v2p31/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r9.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v2p31/r9.claim: Al-Suddī glosses nunshizuhā as moving or stirring the bones.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r1.claim: In the narrated setting, ʿUzayr rests under a tree, leaves his donkey, explores the empty town, eats its figs and grapes, drinks pressed grapes, and falls asleep.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r2.claim: God causes the young ʿUzayr and his donkey to die in sleep, while concealing their bodies from people and animals.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r3.claim: After seventy years, a Persian ruler called Yūshak arrives with a thousand stewards and vast labor crews to rebuild Jerusalem.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r4.claim: The account says Nebuchadnezzar dies from a mosquito in his brain, the surviving Israelites return, and the city flourishes again over thirty years.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r5.claim: After a century, God raises ʿUzayr; the verb بعث suggests his return as before, intelligent and able to reason about divine realities, more fully than the verb أحياه would.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r6.claim: The question about how long he had remained may come from God or a commissioned angel, and is meant to expose the limit of his knowledge and extinguish any sense that the interval was short.

BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337#2/r7.claim: The century-long preservation of food is another extraordinary sign, since food naturally deteriorates.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r1.claim: Delight in worldly possessions signals distance from God; relying on what one holds shows weak trust, and turning to people in hardship shows that one has not truly known God.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r2.speaker: السعدي
BURSEVI:v1p337/r2.claim: Saʿdī's poem reflects on worldly pride and death: rulers die and are buried, and only a good or bad name remains from what each person cultivated.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r3.claim: The supplication asks for long lives joined to good deeds, short hopes, and complete understanding.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r4.claim: The phrase 'or like the one' coordinates with the preceding 'did you not see'; it means 'or did you see someone like this,' using comparison because many reject resurrection and even more doubt how it occurs.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r5.claim: The passerby is ʿUzayr ibn Sharḥiyā, and the ruined town is Jerusalem, the most widely accepted and strongest identification; qarya derives from gathering people.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r6.claim: The historical account says Nebuchadnezzar came with six hundred thousand standards, ruined Jerusalem, killed some Israelites, left some in Syria, and deported others as captives distributed among his kings.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r7.claim: The city lay empty with its roofs collapsed over the walls; the root of خاوية describes an emptied interior or a house that fell in.

BURSEVI:v1p337/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p337/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p337/r8.claim: ʿUzayr asks how God will rebuild the ruined city itself; he is expressing ordinary human astonishment, not doubt in God's power.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r1.claim: A report says the figs and grapes remained as freshly picked and the grape juice as freshly pressed.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r2.claim: The clause about not changing is a circumstantial phrase that can appear with or without a conjunction; food and drink take a singular pronoun because they act as one nourishment.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r3.claim: The hāʾ in لم يتسنه may be a root letter, from سنهة, or a pause hāʾ from سنوة; 'not change' expresses the implication that years have not passed.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r4.claim: The donkey's scattered, broken bones make the long elapsed time visible and reassure ʿUzayr.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r5.claim: God preserves the food and revives ʿUzayr and his donkey as a sign for the people of that century, including a chance to learn Torah knowledge lost across generations.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r6.claim: The repeated command to inspect the bones shifts attention from elapsed time to the process of reviving another body, after ʿUzayr has witnessed his own revival.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r7.claim: The verb ننشزها means lifting and reassembling the bones into their proper places; the clause may describe their living state or stand for their condition.

BURSEVI:v1p338/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p338/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p338/r8.claim: Flesh is singular because the bones are visibly separate while flesh appears connected; the account leaves the breathing of spirit unexplained because it is not needed here.

BURSEVI:v1p339/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p339/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p339/r1.claim: A heavenly voice commands the scattered bones to rejoin; bones, nerves, veins, flesh, skin, and hair return in order, then the spirit is breathed in and the donkey stands braying.

BURSEVI:v1p339/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p339/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p339/r2.claim: After he sees the dead revived, ʿUzayr recognizes that God's power encompasses every possible thing, including the wonders he witnessed.

BURSEVI:v1p339/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p339/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p339/r3.claim: Back home, ʿUzayr finds an old blind, disabled woman who knew him; he prays and restores her sight and mobility, and she recognizes him.

BURSEVI:v1p339/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p339/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p339/r4.claim: His descendants initially doubt the returned ʿUzayr, but his adult son verifies him by a distinctive crescent-shaped black mark between his shoulders.

BURSEVI:v1p339/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p339/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p339/r5.claim: The report says Nebuchadnezzar killed forty thousand Torah reciters, leaving no copy or living expert; ʿUzayr recites it from memory, and a buried manuscript is found and matches him letter for letter.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r1.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو علي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r1.claim: Most grammarians, including al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, and Abū ʿAlī, take kāf as a noun meaning 'like,' governed by an omitted 'have you seen'; the preceding 'have you not seen' signals the omission.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the kāf as extra, yielding a direct coordination with the earlier person who disputed Abraham.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r3.claim: Other grammarians analyze the coordination semantically, as though the text said 'Have you not seen the one who argued—or the one who passed?'; another view makes it Abraham challenging his opponent, which al-Ālūsī finds weak because of the distance and ellipsis.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r4.claim: Direct coordination of the relative clause with the previous relative would require a preposition before kāf; as a noun it rarely accepts one, and as a particle it cannot.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r5.claim: A proposed distinction says 'have you not seen' introduces the object of wonder while 'have you seen' introduces its likeness; al-Ālūsī rejects it because both expressions occur with and without comparison in Arabic and Qurʾanic usage.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r6.claim: The particle aw marks a choice or a detailed alternative, and the passerby is most commonly identified as Ezra.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r7.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p19#2/r7.claim: Ezra son of Sherekhya is reported from ʿAlī by al-Ḥākim and also from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, and numerous early authorities.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r1.speaker: وهب
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r1.claim: Alternative identities are Armiya son of Ḥilqiyā, related by Abū Jaʿfar and favored by Wahb, or al-Khiḍr, related from Ibn Isḥāq; some say Armiya and al-Khiḍr are the same.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r2.claim: Other proposed identities include the prophet Shuʿayā and Lot's servant; Ibn Isḥāq is named for the al-Khiḍr identification.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r3.claim: Mujāhid says the passerby was an unbeliever in resurrection; he cites the narrative's parallel with Nimrod and the apparent wording of incredulity, but the author argues the surrounding context and the unusual event favor a believer instead.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r4.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that the man's shared request to witness revival with Abraham and the extraordinary favor shown him make the unbeliever identification unlikely; his words can express wonder rather than denial.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r5.claim: The village is identified by Ibn Zayd as the town from which thousands departed; other reports name Dayr Sāyir Abād, Dayr Salmābād, Dayr Hiraql, al-Muʾtafikah, or a grape-growing village near Jerusalem.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r6.speaker: عكرمة والربيع ووهب
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r6.claim: ʿIkrimah, al-Rabīʿ, and Wahb identify the village as Jerusalem, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar; al-Ālūsī calls this the best-known view and derives qaryah from gathering.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r7.claim: Khāwiyah ʿalā ʿurūshihā means either collapsed onto its roofs, with roofs falling first, or empty of inhabitants while its houses still stand; he rejects complicated grammatical accounts of the phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r8.claim: The line 'he said' may describe speech inwardly or aloud; the demonstrative may point to the village itself, its inhabitants by ellipsis, or its decayed bones and corpses, with literal or figurative revival accordingly.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p20/r9.claim: On the figurative reading, the passerby longs to see the ruined town rebuilt while sensing despair; on a literal reading, he either acknowledges his inability if a believer or denies the possibility if an unbeliever.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers taking the village itself as the object of revival: the text describes the village rather than its people or bones, and omits any claim that the dead became dust or bones, which would intensify the impossibility.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r2.claim: The fronted object receives emphasis because the wonder concerns the village, not the agent; annā means either 'when' as a temporal adverb or 'how' as a circumstantial phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r3.claim: God's causing him to die for a hundred years means keeping him dead for that duration, since the act of removing life does not itself extend over time; ʿām is linked etymologically to the sun's course.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r4.claim: Baʿath means raising him to life; it suggests swift, easy divine action and that he rose with his faculties intact, prepared to reflect.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r5.claim: A narrative cited from al-Baḥr says that after his death God sent the Persian king Kusk with workers to rebuild Jerusalem; God destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito, Israelites returned, and the restored city flourished before the passerby was revived.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r6.claim: The question 'How long did you remain?' is introduced to expose the man's inability to grasp God's affairs and eliminate his doubts; kam is a temporal accusative with an omitted 'time' as its specification.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r7.claim: The apparent speaker is God, but other views name a heavenly voice, Gabriel, a prophet, or a believing witness who lived from the man's death to his revival; only the last makes attribution to God figurative.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p21/r8.claim: The man estimates that he remained a day or part of one, either by guess or because the interval seemed short; a report says he died in the morning and awoke before sunset, first saying a day then correcting himself after seeing the sun.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r1.claim: God corrects the estimate: he remained a hundred years, not a day or part of one.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r10.claim: Āyah means an instructive sign or guide; its audience may be humanity, the survivors of his people, or contemporaries who see a man from ancient generations and learn the lost Torah from him.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r11.speaker: السدي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r11.claim: Al-Suddī identifies the bones as the donkey's; other reports say they are the dead villagers' or the passerby's own, with his eyes revived first while his body remained dead. Al-Ālūsī dismisses the competing accounts.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r12.claim: With zāy, nunshizuhā means raising the bones from the earth and returning them to their places in the body; al-Kisāʾī glosses it as softening and enlarging them.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r13.speaker: أبي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r13.claim: Ubay reads nunshīhā; Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read nunshiruhā, understood as bringing the dead to life, though al-Ālūsī says life here may mean the prior stages because flesh follows.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r14.speaker: أبان عن عاصم
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r14.claim: Abān from ʿĀṣim reads nunshiruhā with an alternative vocalization meaning to spread or unroll the bones, following al-Farrāʾ.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r15.claim: The phrase about how God raises the bones is parsed either as a circumstantial clause or as an explanatory apposition; although interrogative clauses normally resist circumstantial use, the question here is not literal.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r16.claim: The passage omits how the spirit is breathed into the body because explaining that process does not serve the relevant wisdom.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r17.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r17.claim: An account says an angel called the bones and they assembled from every direction; sinews, flesh, skin, and hair were restored, then spirit entered and the donkey rose braying toward heaven.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r18.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r18.claim: When it became clear to him, he understood the stages of revival; the text omits the obvious assembling and clothing of the bones to emphasize its immediacy.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r2.claim: One opinion says his food was grapes or figs and his drink juice or milk.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r3.claim: Lam yatasannah means the food and drink did not change through the long period; its root is variously tied to the word for year or to clay that has become altered, while unchanged food means it stayed fresh.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r4.claim: The final letter is analyzed either as original hāʾ, as wāw with a pause hāʾ, or as a pause hāʾ after deletion; another account derives the form from lam yatasannan and explains consonant alteration.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r5.claim: The negative clause is circumstantial; its pronoun refers either to food and drink collectively or only to the latter, whose unchanged state implies the former. ʿAbd Allāh and Ubay are cited for variant readings.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r6.claim: The imperative to look at the food may seem to follow from the hundred years, but al-Ālūsī says the man assumed little time because his body had not changed, making the food's preservation still more striking.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r7.claim: An alternative says he was told to inspect quickly spoiling food as proof that God can resurrect; al-Ālūsī calls it strained and less consistent than the explicit mention of the donkey.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r8.claim: The donkey was likely decomposed, with its bones weathered and joints separated; the claim that it remained alive without food or water is unsupported.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p22/r9.claim: Wa-li-najʿalaka is analyzed as a purpose adjunct to an omitted 'we did that,' or as attached to what precedes, with the conjunction treated as extra or as coordination; it means God acted to make him a sign for people.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r1.claim: Some treat tabayyana's implicit subject as governed jointly by tabayyana and aʿlam in a dispute over grammatical coordination; others read it as the event of clarity itself, supported by Ibn ʿAbbās's passive reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r2.claim: The present form aʿlamu suggests continuing knowledge: the thing itself did not change, but its quality changed from inference to direct observation, showing his earlier words expressed ordinary astonishment rather than denial.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r3.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the phrase as an imperative, 'know'; Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly says Ezra was no better than Abraham, since God commanded each to know, and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī also read it as a command.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r4.claim: If read as a command, its speaker may be God, the Prophet, an angel, or the man addressing and reproving himself for his prior astonishment.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p23/r5.claim: A post-revival story says Ezra rode home unrecognized, then found his former blind, disabled servant, now 120; she asked him to pray for restored sight, and he healed her eyes by prayer and touch before the segment breaks.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r1.claim: At God’s command, Ezra restores an Israelite woman’s sight and legs; she recognizes him, and the community verifies his identity by a birthmark.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r2.claim: The Israelites say Ezra alone retained the Torah after Nebuchadnezzar burned it; his father had hidden a copy, which Ezra retrieves as two lights enter his chest and restore his memory.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r3.claim: An alternate report says Ezra recites the Torah perfectly from memory; a descendant of captives then finds his ancestor’s hidden copy, and their texts agree, prompting the claim that Ezra is God’s son.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p24/r4.claim: The Israelites’ claim that Ezra is God’s son is repudiated as utterly transcending divine truth.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r10.claim: Once the resurrection sign became clear, Ezra affirmed ongoing knowledge that God can do everything, including this miracle.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r3.claim: The passerby may be the human intellect crossing the heart, its holy house, or the prophet Ezra; the city is empty of helpful manifestations and collapsed through weak spiritual readiness.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r4.claim: The question about reviving the dead city expresses bewilderment at truth while ignorant and turned toward otherness; the city may also be a ruined physical place.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r5.claim: The hundred-year death may mean prolonged ignorance, a period of eight years and four months or twenty-five years, ascetic death during spiritual discipline, or literal natural death followed by resurrection.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r6.claim: The apparent short day or part of a day reflects how the period of ignorance or spiritual discipline shrinks beside eternal life; in truth he remained one hundred years.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r7.claim: The fig symbolizes universal intelligibles, with particulars latent like its seeds; grapes symbolize particular cognition with material adjuncts, while grape juice signifies love and gnosis and milk beneficial revealed knowledge.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r8.claim: Unchanged food and drink symbolize innate knowledge deposited according to each soul’s capacity: material veils may hide it, but do not erase it, and it reappears when lifted.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p25/r9.claim: The donkey can signify the bodily form carrying the heart, or the outward meaning; bones are powers raised from nature and clothed with growing flesh of gnosis nourished by spiritual witnessing.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r1.speaker: bazıları
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r1.claim: Some grammarians treat the kaf in ka-alladhi as an extra particle for verbal elegance, since a prepositional kaf could not enter after the preceding construction.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r10.claim: Other identifications say the man was Lot's servant or Sha'ya; another view says he began as an unbeliever and believed after being revived.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r11.speaker: Vehb, Katâde, Dahhâk, İkrime, Rebî‘
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r11.claim: These authorities identify the village as Ilya, that is, Jerusalem.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r12.speaker: Dahhâk
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r12.claim: Dahhâk also reports a village two farsakhs from Jerusalem called Karyetü’l-Ineb, or identifies the site as the Holy Land.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r13.speaker: bazıları
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r13.claim: Some identify the village as al-Mu'tafika.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r14.speaker: İbn Zeyd
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r14.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies it with the city of the thousands who fled death, mentioned earlier in the commentary.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r15.speaker: İbn Abbas
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r15.claim: Ibn Abbas places the village at the Monastery of Heraclius beside the Tigris.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r16.speaker: Kelbî
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r16.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the village as Shaburabad.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r17.speaker: Süddî
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r17.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the village as Salmanabad.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r18.claim: The best-known account identifies the man as Uzayr son of Sherehiya and the village as Jerusalem, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's campaign.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r19.claim: The account says Nebuchadnezzar devastated Jerusalem, killing some Israelites, settling some in Syria, and carrying others into captivity; Uzayr later escaped and saw the city ruined.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r2.claim: Other analyses take kaf as a noun meaning like, or connect the phrase by meaning as have you seen someone like this; the semantic link can yield or like this one.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r20.speaker: İbn Abbas
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r20.claim: Ibn Abbas transmits in detail that this account was the occasion of revelation.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r21.claim: Revival miracles are also narrated for the alternative identifications, and the story's general sense may encompass one or several such events.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r22.speaker: müfessirler
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r22.claim: Some commentators read the episode as movement from unbelief's darkness and despair into faith, success, and hope; the author prefers its more apparent contextual sense as a prophetic miracle arising from a believer's grief.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r23.claim: The episode concerns a believer's grief, wish for revival, and confession of limited understanding, not absolute despair that constitutes unbelief.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r24.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r24.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r24.claim: People not hardened in unbelief may still be brought from disbelief to faith and made witnesses to wonders; God's guardianship of believers includes them.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r25.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r25.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r25.claim: The verse's meaning is not restricted to Uzayr or Ermiyâ: the indefinite village and mentally understood comparison allow the account to fit multiple events.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r26.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r26.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r26.claim: The question may ask how, where, or when God will revive the village, expressing a wish for revival alongside uncertainty about its means and timing.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r27.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r27.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r27.claim: It may express a wish for swift revival and grief at being unable to find its path, fearing that God may act too late for the speaker to see.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r28.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r28.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r28.claim: A third possible sense concedes that God can revive it but suspects He will not.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r29.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r29.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r29.claim: A fourth possible sense denies that the dead can return at all; this would be absolute despair and unbelief.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r3.claim: The explicit comparison directs attention to the event and exemplifies analogical and inductive reasoning from particular cases to general knowledge of God's power.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r4.claim: Believers should read the story alongside recurring life and death events rather than as an isolated wonder; every universal law began with one extraordinary event.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r5.claim: The village was a city whose roofs had collapsed, leaving buildings overturned and the place devastated and deserted.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r6.claim: Arsh primarily means roof, but can also designate roofed structures or anything that casts shade, allowing several visual descriptions of the ruin.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r7.speaker: Hazret-i Ali, İbn Abbas, İkrime, Ebü’l-Âliye, Said b. Cübeyr, Katâde, Rebî‘, Dahhâk, Süddî, Mukātil, Süleyman b. Büreyde, Nâciye b. Ka‘b, Sâlim el-Havâs
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r7.claim: These authorities identify the man who passed the ruined village as the prophet Uzayr.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r8.speaker: Vehb, Mücâhid, Abdullah b. Ubeyd b. Umeyr, Bekir b. Mudar
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r8.claim: These authorities identify the man as Jeremiah, Ermiyâ.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r9.speaker: İbn İshak
ELMALILI:2:257-260#4/r9.claim: Ibn Ishaq says that Ermiyâ was Khidr.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r1.claim: Even if the speaker did not intend outright disbelief, the phrase could imply it and become a verbal slip; believers should not despair, though human weakness can diminish hope.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r2.claim: Absolute despair and absolute security are both unbelief: despair cuts off hope in God, while security is arrogant presumption and a kind of separation from Him.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r3.claim: Even prophets may experience grief and a thought resembling lost hope, but divine aid arrives immediately because they are under God's protection.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r4.claim: In such moments believers should cling more firmly to faith, seek help through patience and prayer, avoid despairing panic, and trust God's power to revive after death.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#5/r5.claim: The verse expresses sorrow that draws divine aid, yet its hint of despair is a lapse; God begins relief while the desired result unfolds only after a century as discipline.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r1.claim: God subjected the man to a death lasting one hundred years; a report says he fell asleep and died in sleep while still young.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r10.claim: He was revived as a sign for people, not because his lifespan had ended, so that he could witness and attest to many kinds of resurrection with certainty.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r11.claim: The command to look at the bones may concern his own, the donkey's, both, or bones in general, and calls for sight and insight.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r12.claim: The usual reading means raising and joining the bones in place; Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read nunshiruhā, meaning reviving them.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r13.claim: The bones emerge and reassemble while flesh forms, grows, and covers them, producing a living body.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r14.claim: The body's changing parts and enduring personal identity display death and revival continually; neither the parts nor the whole alone remain fixed, but God's power sustains them.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r15.claim: Life is everything and everything subsists through God's power; ignoring this leaves people unable to understand resurrection even while witnessing its patterns in their own lives.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r16.claim: When the truth became clear, the man affirmed that God has power over everything; Hamza and Kisai read the verb as an imperative, God commanding him to know this certainty.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r17.claim: Sound reason and science should recognize ordinary causes while remembering God's absolute right as the sovereign sustainer; forgetting it narrows thought and leads to denying established miracles.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r2.claim: God then restored him to life with his former intellect, understanding, and capacity to reason about divine knowledge.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r3.claim: A report says that in year seventy a Persian ruler named Yushek reconquered the Holy Land, Nebuchadnezzar died, survivors returned, and Jerusalem was rebuilt over thirty years before Uzayr was revived there.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r4.claim: Uzayr guessed that he had stayed a day or part of one from the lingering memory of waking and sleep, estimating cautiously rather than lying.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r5.claim: Every future moment retains a memory of the past; sleep and death leave an initial, general recollection that links a person to the earlier self.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r6.claim: Without this continuity of memory, an awakened person would think existence had just begun and say he was newly born.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r7.claim: Because life connects past, present, and future, even a hundred-year life seems like a day when it ends; such experiences visibly illustrate the afterlife and resurrection.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r8.claim: God corrects the estimate and tells him to inspect his food and drink, which have not aged or spoiled but remain fresh.

ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:257-260#6/r9.claim: The donkey too is shown as part of the sign of divine power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r1.claim: Other identifications of the passer are Jeremiah son of Hilkiah or Ezra son of Seraiah.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r2.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies him as Ezekiel son of Buzi, a contemporary of Jeremiah and Daniel who was taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar in the early sixth century BCE.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r3.claim: According to his reconstruction, Ezekiel hid Moses' law books, the Ark, and Moses' staff in a Jerusalem well to save them from Nebuchadnezzar, leaving a secret marker for fellow prophets.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r4.claim: Ezekiel later wrote visions of Jewish calamity and hoped-for deliverance through the twenty-fifth year of exile, then disappeared and may have died or been killed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r5.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the Qur'anic event to Ezekiel's dry-bones vision: God revived the prophet around Jerusalem's restoration under Ezra to validate the prophecy and showed him the food, drink, and donkey as a miracle.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r6.claim: The event became a sign for believers, informed saints, or the town's people, who could recognize the man by his traits when he returned after a century.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r7.claim: The passer's question parallels Ezekiel's question whether dry bones can live; the Qur'an adds details about the century-long death that Jewish writings recorded only later.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p35/r8.claim: The bones being reassembled and covered with flesh recalls Ezekiel's prophecy of Israel's restoration; Ibn ʿĀshūr estimates the chronology at roughly a century, around 560 to 458 BCE.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r1.claim: The revival returned the man's soul to his body as a special life; prophets' bodies do not decay, and this extraordinary event differs from resurrection at the Gathering.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r2.claim: He believed he had stayed a day or part of one either through knowledge God imparted or because he remembered sleeping in the morning and waking near evening.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r3.claim: The command to inspect the unchanged food and drink prompts reflection; they may have accompanied him, been placed in an honored grave, or been with him when God caused him to die.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36#2/r4.claim: لم يتسنه means unchanged; it derives from year because years bring change, its final h is radical, and the form أسنت means afflicted by famine, illustrated by a line attributed to Matrūd al-Khuzāʿī or Ibn al-Zibaʿrā.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r1.claim: Khāwiyah means empty of residents and buildings; ʿurūsh are roofs, and collapse from roofs to walls makes the ruin especially complete.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r2.claim: The town is Jerusalem, seen either in a dream or after Babylonian destruction; he prefers the dream, since the passer was exiled with Jehoiachin before Jerusalem fell under Zedekiah eleven years later.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r3.claim: The question how God will revive the town expresses denial and wonder; the narrative's fa does not require death to have occurred at the very moment of the question.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p36/r4.claim: One reported explanation is that the man slept and God caused his death during sleep.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r1.claim: One view says the donkey had decayed until only bones remained, then God revived it before the man's eyes; simply seeing it sufficed as evidence.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r2.claim: God displayed three forms of revival: restoring the man's body by returning its soul, preserving the food, and restoring the donkey; this was a sign for the convinced, and perhaps some elect witnessed it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r3.claim: ولنجعلك آية is coordinated with an implied command to inspect the donkey: the food, drink, and donkey were a sign to him, while his verified person became a sign to others.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r4.claim: The bones may be those of dead humans; alternatively, the definite article can stand for a possessive, making them the donkey's bones and the phrase an appositive to donkey.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r5.claim: Most of the ten readers read ننشرها with rāʾ, meaning revive; Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read ننشزها with zāy, meaning raise, so the readings supply two related senses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p37/r6.claim: The Book of Ezekiel similarly describes bones joining, then being covered with sinew and flesh and finally skin.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r1.claim: The majority read أعلم with hamzat al-qaṭʿ as the man's present-tense statement, renewing knowledge he had previously attained after seeing the sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p38/r2.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read أعلم with hamzat al-waṣl as God's speech; although coordination with the command to look was expected, it is omitted because this statement is the conclusion of the evidence.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r1.claim: His estimate of one day or part of a day reflects death and awakening at different times of day; he thought of the interval as sleep and was unsure whether a night had passed.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r2.claim: His second concern was how disintegrated parts could regain their original form after changing from one state and shape to another.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r3.claim: The author compares this passage with the wording of Moses first receiving revelation, arguing that the passerbys exchange sounds like an ongoing, familiar divine conversation.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r4.claim: He was traveling beyond his own town with a mount, food, and drink, and merely passed the ruined village rather than setting out to visit it.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r5.claim: He points to the dead inhabitants, not to the town's buildings: rebuilding a town is not the extraordinary issue, and mention of graves would be needed if he meant buried corpses.

TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:258-260#4/r6.claim: His question had two concerns: the long interval and the return of dispersed, transformed parts to their former bodily form.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r1.claim: The author distinguishes a roof from an ʿarsh, which includes the roof and its supporting pillars, like a grape trellis.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r2.speaker: المفسرون
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r2.claim: One reported parsing joins “or like the one” to the disputant of Abraham; kāf is nominal, yielding “have you seen the like of the one who passed,” and signals multiple proofs.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r3.speaker: المفسرون
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r3.claim: A second reported parsing treats kāf as extra, making the phrase simply join the passerby to the person who disputed with Abraham.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r4.speaker: المفسرون
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r4.claim: A third reported parsing makes the conjunction semantic: “Have you not seen like the one who disputed … or like the one who passed a town?”

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r5.speaker: المفسرون
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r5.claim: A fourth view makes the phrase part of Abraham's reply to his opponent: if he claims to give life and death, let him revive as the passerby did.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r6.claim: Al-Tabataba'i prefers a semantic conjunction but supplies a different ellipsis: the examples are successive demonstrations of God's guidance, not merely parallel objects of sight.

TABATABAI:2:259#2/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#2/r8.claim: The passerby's story demonstrates a second mode of guidance: God makes the truth known through direct showing and witnessing.

TABATABAI:2:259#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r1.claim: The Qur'an names Abraham out of special honor for him, while often presenting resurrection and death in a deliberately minimizing tone.

TABATABAI:2:259#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r2.claim: “How will God revive this?” means how He will revive the people of the town; this is a metonymy like asking a town in the story of Joseph.

TABATABAI:2:259#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#3/r3.claim: The passerby spoke from astonishment at the magnitude of resurrection, not disbelief; his closing “I know” shows no new conversion from doubt, and prophets cannot doubt resurrection.

TABATABAI:2:259#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r1.claim: He rejects inferring dormancy from resemblance to the Sleepers story; analogy cannot determine a disputed textual indication.

TABATABAI:2:259#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r2.speaker: هذا القائل
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r2.claim: The interpreter deems earthly resurrection impossible without evidence, even while allowing century-long dormancy as a miracle; the author rejects the distinction.

TABATABAI:2:259#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r3.claim: Al-Tabataba'i rejects the dormancy interpretation: analogy with the Sleepers cannot override the plain wording “He caused him to die,” and if century-long dormancy is miraculous, literal death and revival are equally possible.

TABATABAI:2:259#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#4/r4.claim: The context confirms ordinary death and revival through the preceding question, the unchanged provisions, the donkey, and the bones; denying earthly resurrection lacks evidence.

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r1.claim: He had not sensed the passage of time and estimated his stay from daylight, explaining why he guessed one day or part of one.

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r2.claim: The preserved food and drink show that provisions can remain unchanged across the interval; the donkey's bones show its length, while the passerby's unchanged body could otherwise invite doubt.

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r3.claim: The donkey too had died and become bones; scripture's silence about its death reflects its refined decorum.

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r4.claim: God's power is not material or bound by time, so reviving ancient dead is no harder than reviving recent dead.

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r5.claim: The purpose clause “to make you a sign for people” identifies a second goal: the bones are shown to him, while his death and revival also make him a public sign; this explains the order and each repeated “look.”

TABATABAI:2:259#5/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#5/r6.claim: His experience also illustrates how the dead will perceive their interval until resurrection day.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r1.claim: The bones are those of the donkey; nanshizuha means to grow or raise them before clothing them with flesh, directly answering the question about bodily restoration.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r2.claim: Some exegetes take the bones to be bones in living bodies, whose growth and covering with flesh also point to resurrection.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r3.claim: He rejects the living-bones interpretation as forced and unsupported; if the bones were the villagers', they too would share the sign, contrary to the wording's focus on the passerby.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r4.claim: Everything from God's causing the passerby to die through the end of the verse is one complete answer to his single question about revival.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r5.claim: After the demonstration, he returns to his prior knowledge of God's absolute power; the passing thought did not mean that he had doubted or newly learned the doctrine.

TABATABAI:2:259#6/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259#6/r6.claim: A reading in which he first doubted God's power and only learned it afterward is impossible: he was a prophet, and the text would say “I knew”; seeing one revival would not establish power over everything except as unreliable astonishment.

TABATABAI:2:259-260/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r1.claim: The three proofs can be framed as three successive examples, three types of guidance, or a command to recall each story; all fit the context.

TABATABAI:2:259-260/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r2.claim: God varies the three rhetorical patterns across these verses to stimulate attention and realize all the contextual benefits available.

TABATABAI:2:259-260/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r3.claim: The ellipsis before the passerby means either like the one who disputed with Abraham or like the one who passed the town.

TABATABAI:2:259-260/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259-260/r5.claim: The passerby, town, former inhabitants, and intended audience are unnamed to downplay an extraordinary resurrection and soften the audience's amazement; other incidental story details are likewise omitted.

TABATABAI:2:259/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259/r1.claim: The Qur'an's confirmation of truth means its effects become established; nullifying falsehood means its corruption appears and its disguise as truth is removed.

TABATABAI:2:259/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259/r2.claim: God's statement that He misguides wrongdoers means they seek the effects of truth by wrongful, false routes and therefore cannot attain them.

TABATABAI:2:259/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259/r3.claim: An oppressor cannot succeed through oppression or reach what the beneficent and God-fearing attain through beneficence and piety.

TABATABAI:2:259/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:259/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:259/r4.claim: The Qur'an's most comprehensive illustration of enduring truth and vanishing falsehood is the flood's foam and the lasting benefit in the earth; causality and repeated experience confirm the principle.

ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n252/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n252/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n252/r1.claim: Asad's bracketed words follow Zamakhshari, who connects this verse's opening with the preceding verse.

ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r1.claim: Asad reads the story as a parable of resurrection, placed between Abraham's statement that God gives life and death and his request to see resurrection; claims identifying the man and town lack basis and may reflect Talmudic legends.

ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n253/r2.claim: Speculations by earlier commentators identifying the man and town are baseless and may have been influenced by Talmudic legends.

ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n254/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n254/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n254/r1.claim: The preserved food implies that it remains alive, showing God's power to sustain life indefinitely as well as resurrect the dead.

ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n255/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n255/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:259#n255/r1.claim: The recurring birth process, including the embryo's gradual development, visibly demonstrates God's power to create and recreate life.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r1.claim: The ruined-town episode is the second example after Abraham's debate with Nimrod: the first addresses shirk and denial, while this one corrects denial of resurrection.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r2.speaker: İslâmî kaynaklar
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r2.claim: The town is identified as Jerusalem, and the visitor is identified in differing reports as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah or Uzair son of Sharyah (Ezra son of Seraiah).

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r3.speaker: İbn Âشûr
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r3.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers identifying the visitor as the Israelite prophet Ezekiel, who lived in the same period as Jeremiah and Daniel.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r4.claim: Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE and deported its people; Ezekiel hid sacred Mosaic relics in a well before exile and later wrote revelation-based texts in Babylon.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r5.claim: Ezekiel died around 560 BCE and Jerusalem was rebuilt around 458 BCE under Uzair, roughly a century later; God then revived Ezekiel and showed him revived bones, preserved food and drink, and his restored donkey as a sign of resurrection and the afterlife.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r6.claim: The Ethiopic Baruch account says Abdel-Melek slept 66 years, awoke after the Babylonian exile to rebuilt Jerusalem, and found his bread and figs still fresh.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:259/r7.claim: God guides through rational arguments, by showing what a reported event was like, or by making people experience cause and effect; Abraham, Ezekiel, and the next verse illustrate these methods.

QIRAAT-ER:2:259:22#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:22#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:22#1/r1.claim: Hamzah is dropped for easier pronunciation without changing the meaning.

QIRAAT-ER:2:259:38#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:38#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:38#1/r1.claim: This repeats the hamzah-dropping variant already noted for word 22.

QIRAAT-ER:2:259:47#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:47#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:47#1/r1.claim: The form without final hāʾ supports root s-n-w, while the form with it supports s-n-h; the canonical split encodes that root dispute.

QIRAAT-ER:2:259:63#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:63#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:63#1/r1.claim: The reading changes the root from n-sh-z to n-sh-r, meaning spread or resurrect rather than raise.

QIRAAT-ER:2:259:72#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:72#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:259:72#1/r1.claim: The imperative means God commands the man to know, rather than the man declaring his knowledge.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r1.speaker: Commentators
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r1.claim: Commentators typically identify the man who passed the ruined town as Ezra.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r10.claim: If the man was a prophet, his question expresses a wish to see resurrection, like Abraham’s question in the next verse, rather than pernicious doubt.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r2.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r2.claim: Other identifications name Ezekiel or Khiḍr.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r3.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r3.claim: Some interpret the figure as an ordinary disbeliever shown the reality of resurrection, rather than a saint or prophet.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r4.claim: The town’s roofs had collapsed and its walls fallen on them; khāwiyah also suggests emptiness.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r5.claim: The question about how long he tarried recurs in the sleepers’ account and in a soul’s questioning on Judgment Day.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r6.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r6.claim: Some say the donkey’s bones were revived and clothed with flesh.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r7.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r7.claim: Others take the bones being reassembled and clothed to refer to the man himself.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r8.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r8.claim: Some infer that being made a sign means the man was made a prophet.

STUDYQURAN:2:259/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:259/r9.claim: Being a sign does not establish prophethood, since Pharaoh too was made a sign and was no prophet.
